  ---------------------------------------------------------------
  PHASE 1: SPREADSHEETS DONE PROPERLY
  ---------------------------------------------------------------
  The foundation almost everyone half-knows, rebuilt so the later work holds up.

    Month 1: Excel and Google Sheets Foundations (Weeks 1-4)
      Structuring Data So It Can Be Analysed
        Topics:
          - What a clean table actually looks like, and why yours probably is not one
          - Rows as records, columns as fields, and one fact per cell
          - Why merged cells and colour-as-data destroy analysis
          - Data types, dates and the formatting traps that silently break totals
          - Turning a human-formatted sheet into an analysable one
        Projects built:
          - Take a genuinely badly structured sheet and restructure it into a usable table
        Practice: Restructure three messy real-world sheets
      The Formulas That Actually Matter
        Topics:
          - Absolute and relative references, and why formulas break when copied
          - IF, nested conditions, and when to stop nesting
          - SUMIF, COUNTIF, AVERAGEIF and their multi-criteria versions
          - Text and date functions for real cleanup
          - Error handling so a broken cell does not poison a whole column
        Projects built:
          - Build a summary sheet driven entirely by formulas from a raw data tab
        Practice: 20 formula tasks against a real dataset
      Lookups and Joining Data
        Topics:
          - VLOOKUP, XLOOKUP and INDEX with MATCH, and when each is right
          - Joining two tables on a common key
          - Handling missing matches honestly instead of hiding them
          - Duplicate keys and the quiet damage they do
          - The equivalents in Google Sheets
        Projects built:
          - Combine three separate exports into one analysable table and reconcile the mismatches
        Practice: 15 lookup and join exercises including deliberately broken keys
        Assessment: A timed spreadsheet task: clean, join and summarise a real dataset
      Pivot Tables and Fast Summaries
        Topics:
          - Pivot tables from the ground up
          - Grouping, filtering and calculated fields
          - Slicing by dimension to find where a number actually comes from
          - Reading a pivot critically instead of accepting it
          - Charts that clarify rather than decorate
        Projects built:
          - Answer five real business questions about one dataset using only pivots
        Practice: Build pivots answering supplied questions, then explain each finding

  ---------------------------------------------------------------
  PHASE 2: CLEANING REAL DATA AND ANALYSING IT HONESTLY
  ---------------------------------------------------------------
  Where most analysis fails, and the statistics you need to avoid fooling yourself.

    Month 2: Data Cleaning and Practical Statistics (Weeks 5-8)
      Cleaning Messy Real Data
        Topics:
          - Duplicates, near-duplicates and how to decide which is real
          - Missing values and the options: exclude, impute or report
          - Inconsistent categories and text normalisation
          - Outliers, and telling a data error from a genuine extreme
          - Documenting every cleaning decision so your numbers are defensible
        Projects built:
          - Clean a genuinely messy dataset and write a short log of every decision made
        Practice: Clean three datasets with different problems
      Power Query for Repeatable Cleaning
        Topics:
          - Why manual cleaning does not survive next month's file
          - Power Query basics: importing, transforming and loading
          - Building a repeatable cleaning pipeline
          - Unpivoting and reshaping data
          - Refreshing when new data arrives, with no rework
        Projects built:
          - Build a Power Query pipeline that cleans a monthly export automatically
        Practice: Convert last week's manual cleaning into a repeatable query
      Statistics That Keep You Honest
        Topics:
          - Mean, median and when the average actively misleads
          - Spread and why two datasets with the same average differ completely
          - Percentages, percentage points and the errors that get presented in meetings
          - Correlation is not causation, with real examples
          - Sample size and why small numbers should not drive big decisions
        Projects built:
          - Take a real claim from a report and check whether the data actually supports it
        Practice: Critique supplied analyses and identify what each gets wrong
        Assessment: A written critique of a deliberately misleading analysis
      Charts That Do Not Lie
        Topics:
          - Choosing the chart from the question, not from preference
          - Truncated axes and the other ways charts mislead
          - Comparing like with like
          - Labelling so a chart survives being forwarded without you
          - Removing everything that is not carrying information
        Projects built:
          - Redesign three bad charts and explain what each change fixes
        Practice: Build charts for supplied questions and defend each choice

          - Fact and dimension tables in plain language
          - Relationships and why a star schema keeps numbers correct

          - Date tables and time intelligence
          - Diagnosing a wrong total caused by a bad relationship
        Projects built:

        Practice: Fix three broken data models
      DAX Measures Without Fear
        Topics:
          - Calculated columns versus measures, and why the difference matters

        Practice: Complete supplied tasks with AI, then verify every output
      Checking What AI Gives You
        Topics:
          - Why an AI can produce a confident, plausible, wrong formula

          - Spot-checking summaries against the raw data

          - Being able to explain any number you present, whatever produced it

        Assessment: A verification test: find every error in an AI-assisted analysis

          - Sourcing and cleaning the data end to end

COMMON QUESTIONS ABOUT THIS COURSE

  For anything about cost, use PART 4 and RULE 1. Do not quote two regions.

  Q: What does this data science course cover?
  A: The full pipeline in order: Python with NumPy and Pandas, statistics, data visualization,
  SQL and exploratory data analysis with feature engineering; then machine learning,
  regression, classification, ensembles and unsupervised methods with honest evaluation,
  end-to-end projects and Kaggle practice; then deep learning, neural networks, CNNs, RNNs,
  NLP, applied computer vision and a research-paper implementation. A finale month ships a
  deployed capstone and sits the final exam.

  Q: How long does it take to learn data science properly?
  A: Ten months of teaching at 2 live classes a week plus 4 to 6 hours of practice, with two
  more months in hand for learners who need them. The three teaching phases build the skill and
  its real-world application; the finale month ships a capstone and sits the final exam.

  Q: How am I assessed? Is the certificate just for attending?
  A: No. Problem sets follow every class with written feedback, monthly reviews deliberately
  mix new material with earlier topics, each phase ends with a cumulative exam, and the course
  ends with a final exam: a practical build plus written questions from the whole syllabus.
  Passing earns the certificate; falling short earns focused revision and a free retest.

  Q: How is this different from your data analysis and AI/ML courses?
  A: Three different jobs. Data analysis is the business-facing craft: Excel, SQL, dashboards
  and clear answers to business questions. This data science course is the full modelling
  pipeline: statistics, machine learning and deep learning on top of that data craft. The AI/ML
  engineering course goes deepest into models and the systems that serve them. If you want the
  classic data scientist profile, this is the course; the other two are its neighbours.

  Q: Do I need strong maths before joining?
  A: No: school-level comfort with numbers is enough to start, and the statistics you need is
  taught inside the course, in code, on real data. What we do not do is hide the maths that
  matters: probability, distributions and evaluation metrics are taught properly because
  interviews and real work both reach for them.

COURSE 49 OF 122: DATA SCIENCE FOR TEENS: PYTHON & YOUR FIRST ML MODELS
====================================================================================================

Course link: https://learn.modernagecoders.com/courses/data-science-course-for-teens-python-data
Subject area: Data Science
Designed for: Teens
Who can join: Ages 14 to 18, basic Python required
Course length: 6 months (24 weeks)
Time needed: 2 live classes/week + 2-3 hours practice
Certificate: Certificate from Modern Age Coders, awarded on passing the final assessment

PRICE FOR THIS COURSE (quote only the one that applies to the person asking)
  In India, per month:      group Rs 1,499, mini batch Rs 2,999, one to one Rs 4,999
  Outside India, per month: group $100, one to one $150
  Classes: group and mini batch two live classes a week, eight a month; one to one in India one
  live class a week, four a month; one to one outside India two live classes a week, eight a
  month. Each class is one hour.

WHAT THIS COURSE IS

  Live online data science course for teens (14-18): pandas, cleaning real datasets,
  matplotlib, statistics and your first ML models with scikit-learn.

  In one line: Real datasets, honest charts, and a first machine learning model that the student can actually explain.

ABOUT THE PROGRAMME

  Data science is the rare school-age subject where the professional tools are free and the
  real material, actual datasets about movies, sport, cities, and climate, is sitting in public
  archives waiting to be questioned. This 6-month live course teaches teens to do the real
  thing: load data with pandas, clean it honestly, chart it with matplotlib without lying,
  reason about it with statistics, and finally train first machine learning models with
  scikit-learn and understand what they did. The course is deliberately anti-hype. Students
  learn that most of data science is careful cleaning and honest questions, that a chart can
  mislead and how not to let it, and that a model is only as good as the data and the person
  reading its results. It ends with a data-story capstone: each student picks a question they
  care about, finds the data, does the analysis end to end, and presents a notebook that shows
  their reasoning. Basic Python is required; our Python for Teens course is the natural on-ramp
  for students who need it.

WHAT MAKES THIS COURSE DIFFERENT

  - Real public datasets from the second month: movies, sports seasons, city open data, and
    climate records, not sanitized textbook tables
  - A whole month on cleaning, because that is the actual job, and students learn to log every
    cleaning decision like professionals
  - Honest charts are treated as an ethical skill: a full lesson on how visualizations mislead
    and how to avoid it
  - Statistics taught for use, not for the exam: when the mean lies, what correlation does not
    prove
  - Machine learning arrives late and lands properly: train-test splits and simple models the
    student can explain, not black-box demos
  - The capstone is a question the student chose, answered end to end in a notebook they present
    and publish

THE LEARNING PATH, STEP BY STEP

  Phase 1: Python tuned for data, then pandas: loading, filtering, grouping, and joining real
  datasets until table thinking is second nature
  Phase 2: The craft: a full month cleaning genuinely messy data, then matplotlib and the
  discipline of charts that tell the truth
  Phase 3: Statistics for judgment, first models with scikit-learn, and a capstone data story
  built from a question the student chose

WHAT A STUDENT NEEDS BEFORE STARTING

  Python basics: Required: variables, loops, functions, and lists. Our Python for Teens course
    is the natural on-ramp if these are missing
  Mathematics: Comfortable school maths. All statistics used is taught inside the course; no
    calculus is needed
  Equipment: A computer with a modern browser and stable internet. Google Colab means nothing
    heavy is installed
  Age: 14 to 18, matched to the reasoning and statistics content

WHO THIS COURSE IS FOR

  Python graduates: Teens who finished a first Python course and want to apply it to something
    real rather than more syntax
  Question askers: Students who argue from evidence and want the tools to find it themselves
  Future stem students: Teens heading toward engineering, economics, or science degrees where
    this exact stack appears in year one
  Sports and stats fans: Students who already read tables of standings and averages for fun and
    want to compute their own
  Portfolio builders: Teens who want a published, defensible piece of analysis to show teachers
    and admissions offices

FULL CURRICULUM, WEEK BY WEEK

  This is the complete teaching plan. Parents can ask about any week.

  ---------------------------------------------------------------
  PHASE 1: PYTHON FOR DATA AND THE PANDAS TOOLKIT (MONTHS 1-2, WEEKS 1-8)
  ---------------------------------------------------------------
  First the Python muscles data work leans on, retrained in notebooks. Then pandas, the tool
  that turns tables of raw data into answers.

    Month 1: Python, Retuned for Data (Weeks 1-4)
      Notebooks and the Python Refresh
        Topics:
          - Google Colab and Jupyter notebooks: why data work lives in cells, not scripts
          - Refresh: variables, lists, and dictionaries through data-flavored exercises
          - Refresh: loops and conditionals over collections of records
          - Markdown cells: notes and reasoning next to code
          - Notebook habits: run order, restarts, and the stale-state trap
          - The course map: where pandas, charts, and models fit
        Projects built:
          - Class survey analysis, round one: collect a small class survey and answer three questions
            about it with plain Python
        Practice: 12 refresh exercises on lists and dictionaries, all phrased as data questions
      Functions and Files
        Topics:
          - Refresh: writing and calling functions that transform data
          - Reading files: opening a CSV by hand with the csv module
          - What a CSV actually is: rows, delimiters, and headers
          - Building lists of dictionaries from raw rows
          - Writing results back out to a file
          - Why this manual work matters: understanding what pandas automates
        Projects built:
          - Hand-rolled report: read a 500-row CSV with plain Python and compute totals, averages, and a
            top-five list
        Practice: Write three reusable functions: load a CSV, filter rows by a condition,
        summarize a column
      Thinking in Tables
        Topics:
          - Rows as records, columns as variables: the table mental model
          - Data types in the wild: numbers, text, dates, and categories
          - First contact with messy data: a deliberately imperfect dataset
          - Questions data can answer, and questions it cannot
          - From question to query: translating curiosity into precise operations
          - Sources of real data: open data portals and public archives, toured live
        Projects built:
          - Question workshop: pick a public dataset, write five precise questions about it, and classify
            which are answerable from the columns present
        Practice: Find one dataset about something you personally care about and describe its
        rows, columns, and types
      NumPy Essentials
        Topics:
          - Arrays vs lists: what NumPy is for
          - Vectorized operations: arithmetic on whole columns at once
          - Useful reductions: sum, mean, min, max, and where they mislead
          - Boolean masks: selecting data with conditions, the idea pandas is built on
          - A speed demonstration: the same computation with a loop and with NumPy
          - Reading NumPy errors without panic
        Projects built:
          - Class survey analysis, round two: redo week 1's analysis in NumPy and compare the code side
            by side
        Practice: 10 NumPy exercises: masks, reductions, and column arithmetic on a provided
        dataset
        Assessment: Month 1 check: live notebook exercise combining functions, file reading,
        and NumPy on a fresh dataset

    Month 2: pandas (Weeks 5-8)
      DataFrames
        Topics:
          - Series and DataFrames: pandas's two shapes
          - Loading CSVs with read_csv and its most useful options
          - First-look tools: head, info, describe, and shape
          - Selecting columns and rows: loc and iloc without the usual confusion
          - Column arithmetic: creating new columns from old ones
          - Saving your work: to_csv and keeping raw data untouched
        Projects built:
          - First pandas notebook: load a movies dataset and produce a profile of it, size, columns,
            types, and five first findings
        Practice: Load three different datasets and write a three-line profile of each
      Filtering and Sorting
        Topics:
          - Boolean masks in pandas: rows matching a condition
          - Combining conditions: and, or, and the parentheses that matter
          - isin, between, and string contains for readable filters
          - Sorting by one and several columns
          - nlargest and nsmallest: top-N questions answered directly
          - Chaining operations without losing readability
        Projects built:
          - Movie interrogation: answer ten ranked questions about the movies dataset, best-rated per
            decade, longest, most profitable, each as a clean filtered result
        Practice: Write and answer eight filter questions of your own on a sports dataset
      Grouping and Aggregation
        Topics:
          - value_counts: the fastest first answer in pandas
          - groupby: split, apply, combine, drawn before coded
          - Aggregations: mean, sum, count, and multiple at once with agg
          - Grouping by more than one column
          - Sorting grouped results to find leaders and outliers
          - Pivot tables, gently: the spreadsheet idea in pandas form
        Projects built:
          - Season in review: full statistical breakdown of a sports season, per team and per month, from
            a raw match-results dataset
        Practice: Answer six groupby questions on a dataset of your choice and mark the most
        surprising result
      Combining Datasets
        Topics:
          - concat: stacking datasets that share columns
          - merge: joining tables on a shared key, with the four join types in pictures
          - What gets lost in a join: rows that match nothing
          - Checking a merge: row counts before and after
          - Tidying column names and types after combining
          - The month project workflow: load, join, group, answer
        Projects built:
          - Two-table analysis: join two related datasets, for example city populations with air quality
            readings, and answer three questions no single table could
        Practice: Perform one merge on new data and write two sentences on rows that failed to
        match and why
        Assessment: Month 2 check: timed pandas practical, six questions on an unseen dataset,
        filters through joins

  ---------------------------------------------------------------
  PHASE 2: CLEANING REAL DATA AND CHARTING IT HONESTLY (MONTHS 3-4, WEEKS 9-16)
  ---------------------------------------------------------------
  The craft phase. Real datasets arrive dirty, and most of data science is the disciplined work
  of fixing them, then showing results without distortion.

    Month 3: Cleaning Real Datasets (Weeks 9-12)
      Missing Values
        Topics:
          - Finding the holes: isna, counts, and missingness patterns
          - Why data goes missing, and why the reason changes the fix
          - Dropping rows or columns: when it is honest and when it hides too much
          - Filling values: constants, means, medians, and the trade-offs of each
          - The cleaning log: recording every decision and its justification
          - Raw data stays raw: cleaned copies, never overwritten originals
        Projects built:
          - Missing-value audit: map the missingness of a real open dataset, choose treatments per
            column, and defend each in your cleaning log
        Practice: Apply two different missing-value strategies to the same column and compare
        how the summary statistics move
      Wrong Types and Dirty Strings
        Topics:
          - Numbers trapped in text: currency symbols, commas, and units
          - String repair with .str methods: strip, replace, lower, split
          - Dates done right: to_datetime and what it makes possible
          - Categories with typos: Delhi, delhi, and DELHI as one value
          - astype and coercion errors: reading what pandas is telling you
          - A repair pipeline: ordered, rerunnable cleaning steps in one notebook section
        Projects built:
          - Type rescue: take a scraped price-and-date dataset where every column is text and restore
            true types, documenting each repair
        Practice: Fix eight prepared dirty columns, one repair function each
      Outliers, Duplicates, and Judgment Calls
        Topics:
          - Spotting outliers: sorting, describe, and quick plots
          - Error or truth: the 190-year-old customer vs the genuine billionaire
          - Duplicates: exact, partial, and the drop_duplicates decisions
          - The ethics of cleaning: every removal changes the conclusion
          - Documenting judgment calls so others can disagree with you fairly
          - Sanity checks: totals and counts that must still make sense after cleaning
        Projects built:
          - Judgment file: on a dataset seeded with ambiguous outliers and duplicates, decide keep or
            remove case by case, with one-line justifications
        Practice: Trade judgment files with a classmate and write where you disagreed and why
      The Cleaning Project
        Topics:
          - A genuinely messy public dataset, start to finish
          - Planning the clean: audit first, repair second, verify third
          - Combining the month: missingness, types, strings, outliers, duplicates
          - Writing the cleaning log as a professional document
          - Before-and-after: quantifying what the clean changed
          - Delivering an analysis-ready dataset someone else could trust
        Projects built:
          - Full cleaning project: raw city open data, for example street trees or road accidents, taken
            from download to documented, analysis-ready form
        Practice: Run your cleaned dataset through five sanity checks and record the results
        Assessment: Month 3 check: cleaning log review plus a defense of three judgment calls
        in a short viva

    Month 4: Visualization with matplotlib (Weeks 13-16)
      First Charts
        Topics:
          - The anatomy of a figure: axes, ticks, labels, title, legend
          - Line charts: change over time, done cleanly
          - Bar charts: comparing categories without clutter
          - Scatter plots: two variables meeting for the first time
          - Labeling as a duty: a chart must explain itself
          - Plotting straight from pandas, and when to drop to matplotlib
        Projects built:
          - Three-chart notebook: one line, one bar, one scatter from your cleaned month 3 dataset, each
            fully labeled
        Practice: Recreate two published charts from their underlying data as closely as you
        can
      Distributions and the Right Chart
        Topics:
          - Histograms: seeing the shape of a column
          - Bin sizes and how they change the story
          - Box plots: medians, quartiles, and outliers at a glance
          - Comparing groups: side-by-side boxes and grouped bars
          - Choosing the chart from the question, not from habit
          - The chart-choice checklist: comparison, trend, distribution, relationship
        Projects built:
          - Distribution study: profile three numeric columns with histograms and box plots, and write
            what each shape reveals
        Practice: For six written questions, name the right chart type and justify it in one
        line each
      Honest Charts and Polished Figures
        Topics:
          - How charts mislead: truncated axes, cherry-picked windows, and area tricks
          - Fixing a misleading chart without hiding the real pattern
          - Multi-panel figures with subplots
          - Color with intent: highlighting one series, not decorating all of them
          - Annotating the point: arrows and text that guide the reader
          - Exporting print-quality figures
        Projects built:
          - Mislead and repair: take one truthful chart, make the most misleading legal version of it,
            then write the repair, a before-and-after pair
        Practice: Find one misleading chart in real media and write a three-sentence critique
      The Four-Chart Data Story
        Topics:
          - Narrative order: charts arranged as an argument
          - One message per chart: trimming everything else
          - Writing connective text between figures
          - The takeaway figure: your single most important chart
          - Presenting figures aloud: saying what to look at
          - Peer review: reading a classmate's story cold
        Projects built:
          - Mini data story: a four-chart narrative on a dataset of your choice, presented live in five
            minutes
        Practice: Revise your story after peer feedback and note the two changes that most
        improved it
        Assessment: Month 4 check: data story presentation, graded on chart choice, honesty,
        and clarity

  ---------------------------------------------------------------
  PHASE 3: STATISTICS, FIRST MODELS, AND THE CAPSTONE (MONTHS 5-6, WEEKS 17-24)
  ---------------------------------------------------------------
  Statistics gives judgment, scikit-learn gives first models, and the capstone puts it all
  behind one question the student actually cares about.

    Month 5: Statistics for Judgment, Then First Models (Weeks 17-20)
      Describing Data Truthfully
        Topics:
          - Mean, median, and mode: three centers, three stories
          - When the mean lies: income, house prices, and skew
          - Spread: range, quartiles, and standard deviation as a feel, not a formula
          - Percentiles: where a value really stands
          - Summaries that hide things: same mean, wildly different data
          - Writing statistical sentences that a non-technical reader cannot misread
        Projects built:
          - Two-summary exercise: describe the same real dataset once to flatter it and once to be fair,
            then annotate the tricks in the flattering version
        Practice: Compute and interpret full summaries for three columns of your
        capstone-candidate dataset
      Correlation and Its Traps
        Topics:
          - Correlation as a number: direction and strength on a scatter plot
          - Computing correlations in pandas and reading a correlation matrix
          - Correlation is not causation: the argument, with famous spurious examples
          - Confounders: the hidden third variable, explained through cases
          - When correlation is still useful despite the traps
          - Reporting a relationship without overclaiming it
        Projects built:
          - Correlation hunt: find the three strongest relationships in a real dataset, then argue for
            each whether causation is even plausible
        Practice: Find one spurious correlation in the wild or in the class archive and explain
        the likely confounder
      First Machine Learning: Regression
        Topics:
          - What learning from data means, without mystique
          - Features and targets: framing a prediction question
          - The train-test split: why we grade models on unseen data
          - Linear regression with scikit-learn: fit, predict, inspect
          - Reading the model: coefficients as the story it learned
          - Error metrics that mean something: how wrong is the model, in real units
        Projects built:
          - Price predictor: train a linear regression on a real housing or used-car dataset and report
            its typical error honestly
        Practice: Add one feature to your model, remeasure the error, and write whether it
        earned its place
      First Machine Learning: Classification
        Topics:
          - Classification vs regression: predicting a label instead of a number
          - k-nearest neighbors: the friendliest first classifier
          - Decision trees: models you can read as rules
          - Accuracy and its limits: the imbalanced-classes trap
          - The confusion matrix: seeing which mistakes the model makes
          - Overfitting: memorizing vs learning, in one intuitive demonstration
        Projects built:
          - Penguin classifier: train and compare k-nearest neighbors and a decision tree on the Palmer
            Penguins dataset, with a confusion matrix for each
        Practice: Break your classifier on purpose by shrinking training data, and chart
        accuracy against training size
        Assessment: Month 5 check: statistics and modeling quiz plus a live reading of your own
        model's results

    Month 6: The Capstone Data Story (Weeks 21-24)
      The Question and the Data
        Topics:
          - Choosing a question you actually care about: sport, music, games, city, climate

          - Scoping to six weeks of classes: the honest project plan

      The Optional Model and the Narrative

        Practice: Run your dry-run presentation for a family member and note the question that

      Present and Publish

          - Publishing the notebook to GitHub so it has a public address

        Projects built:

        Assessment: Capstone assessment: presentation, notebook quality, cleaning log, and
        honesty of claims

COMMON QUESTIONS ABOUT THIS COURSE

  For anything about cost, use PART 4 and RULE 1. Do not quote two regions.

  Q: Does my teen need to know Python before this course?
  A: Yes, the basics: variables, loops, functions, and lists. Month 1 includes a structured
  refresh, but it assumes prior exposure rather than teaching Python from zero. Students
  without that background should take our Python for Teens course first; it is the natural
  on-ramp, and many students move straight from one into the other.

  Q: How much mathematics does the course require?
  A: Comfortable school maths is enough. Every statistical idea the course uses, means and
  medians, spread, percentiles, correlation, is taught inside the course with real data, and
  there is no calculus anywhere. The emphasis is on judgment: knowing when an average misleads
  matters far more here than deriving formulas.

  Q: Is this real machine learning or just a demo?
  A: Real, at an honest first level. Students train linear regression and classification models
  on real datasets with scikit-learn, use proper train-test splits, read confusion matrices,
  and meet overfitting directly. What we deliberately avoid is black-box theatre: no pasting
  magic code that scores well unexplained. A student finishing this course can tell you what
  their model learned and how wrong it typically is, which is more than many adults using these
  tools can.

  Q: What datasets will my teen work with?
  A: Real public data throughout: movie databases, sports seasons, city open data such as
  street trees and road accidents, climate records, and the Palmer Penguins dataset for
  classification. From month 3 the data arrives genuinely messy on purpose, because cleaning
  real data is the core professional skill. For the capstone, students choose their own dataset
  around a question they care about.

  Q: What does the capstone involve?
  A: Each student picks a question, finds a suitable public dataset, and does the whole job:
  cleaning with a documented log, exploratory analysis, honest figures, an optional model if it
  genuinely helps, and a written conclusion with a limitations section. The finished notebook
  is published to GitHub and presented live. It is a genuine piece of analysis with a public
  address, not a classroom-only exercise.

  Q: How am I assessed, and is the certificate just for showing up?
  A: No. A task follows every class with feedback, monthly reviews deliberately mix new
  material with earlier topics so nothing is forgotten, and the course ends with a final exam
  covering the whole course. Passing earns the certificate; falling short earns focused
  revision and a free retest. We measure real learning, not attendance.

  Q: How are the classes taught?
  A: Live one-hour online classes, twice a week, in small groups capped at 10 students.
  Students work in their own notebooks during class rather than watching, and homework
  notebooks come back with written feedback. Mini-batch (3 to 4 students) and personal 1-on-1
  options are available for students who want closer attention.

  Q: Where does a teen go after this course?
  A: The most common next step is our AI and machine learning track, which starts exactly where
  the scikit-learn month ends. Students leaning toward engineering deepen their Python with our
  advanced courses, and many put the skills straight to work in school science fairs and
  statistics projects. The capstone notebook also carries weight on its own as evidence of real
  analytical work for college applications.

ABOUT THE PROGRAMME

  DSA is the great filter of technical hiring: the same topics appear in every serious
  interview, and the gap between having seen a problem and being able to solve a new one live
  is exactly what interviewers probe. This live online masterclass closes that gap the honest
  way, no memorized solution lists. It builds the full canon in order: complexity analysis and
  linear structures, searching, sorting and hashing, trees, heaps and graphs, then the hard
  middle, shortest paths, network flow, dynamic programming to real depth, greedy and
  backtracking, then interview mastery: company-style problem sets, timed simulations, and
  explaining your reasoning aloud the way the room demands. A finale month runs a
  mock-interview gauntlet and sits the final exam. The pace is honest: ten teaching months at
  two live classes a week plus four to six hours of problem-solving, with two more in hand.
  Problem sets after every class, monthly mixed reviews, phase exams, and a final exam that
  decides the certificate with a free retest.

WHAT MAKES THIS COURSE DIFFERENT

  - Patterns, not memorization: you learn to solve unseen problems, which is the actual test
  - Explaining aloud is trained, not assumed: interviews score communication too
  - Dynamic programming taught until it clicks, the topic that breaks most candidates
  - Company-style problem sets and timed mock interviews, honestly framed as practice
  - An honest 10-month arc with 2 months in hand
  - Real assessment: weekly problem sets, monthly mixed reviews, phase exams and a final exam
    with a free retest

COMMON QUESTIONS ABOUT THIS COURSE

  For anything about cost, use PART 4 and RULE 1. Do not quote two regions.

  Q: What does this DSA course cover?
  A: The full interview canon in order: complexity analysis, arrays, strings, linked lists,
  recursion, stacks and queues, searching, sorting, hashing, trees, heaps, tries and graphs;
  then the hard algorithms, shortest paths, minimum spanning trees, network flow, dynamic
  programming to real depth, greedy and backtracking; then interview mastery with company-style
  problem sets, timed simulations and communication practice. A finale month runs a
  mock-interview gauntlet and sits the final exam.

  Q: How long does it take to learn data structures and algorithms properly?
  A: Ten months of teaching at 2 live classes a week plus 4 to 6 hours of practice, with two
  more months in hand for learners who need them. The three teaching phases build the skill and
  its real-world application; the finale month ships a capstone and sits the final exam.

  Q: How am I assessed? Is the certificate just for attending?
  A: No. Problem sets follow every class with written feedback, monthly reviews deliberately
  mix new material with earlier topics, each phase ends with a cumulative exam, and the course
  ends with a final exam: a practical build plus written questions from the whole syllabus.
  Passing earns the certificate; falling short earns focused revision and a free retest.

  Q: Which language is used for DSA here?
  A: You solve in the language you will interview in, most commonly C++, Java or Python, and
  the instructor supports all three. DSA is language-agnostic at heart: the patterns matter
  more than the syntax, and we make sure your chosen language never gets in the way of the
  thinking.

  Q: Will this course guarantee me a job?
  A: No honest course can, and we will not pretend otherwise. What this course guarantees is
  genuine problem-solving ability, the specific skill interviews test, built through hundreds
  of solved problems and real mock interviews. We prepare you to earn the offer; we do not sell
  the offer.

  no fixed date. The Priority Live Demo is a guaranteed class today or tomorrow, booked at

  A: Live, always: small groups with a real instructor reading your actual code, never

WHAT THIS COURSE IS

  Live online early math course for ages 4-7: counting, number bonds, shapes and measurement
  taught concrete-first in short, joyful classes. Free demo first.

  In one line: The years that decide whether math becomes a friend. We make it one.

ABOUT THE PROGRAMME

  A 12-month live program for children aged 4-7, the years when a child's whole relationship
  with mathematics is quietly decided. Early math done right is not worksheets; it is counting
  that means something, quantities seen and handled, patterns spotted, shapes built and stories
  solved. Our mentors teach concrete-first in genuinely interactive classes structured as short
  playful segments that respect young attention spans: real objects, ten-frames, games and math
  talk, with the child doing and explaining rather than watching. Children leave this course
  fluent in early number, confident in their own thinking, and, the part parents notice most,
  actually liking math.

WHAT MAKES THIS COURSE DIFFERENT

  - Concrete before abstract, always: quantities are handled, drawn, and only then written as
    symbols
  - Classes built for young attention: an hour of varied segments, games, movement, building,
    story problems, never an hour of sitting still
  - Counting taught with meaning: one-to-one correspondence, cardinality and the ideas most
    programs skip straight past
  - Number bonds and part-whole thinking started early, gently, the foundation everything to age
    18 stands on
  - Math talk from day one: even five-year-olds explain their thinking here, in their own words
  - One dedicated mentor who knows the child, their pace and their spark
  - Parents equipped too: simple everyday math-play prompts, because kitchens teach more than
    worksheets
  - The honest opposite of drill academies, no pressure, no rankings, no tears

THE LEARNING PATH, STEP BY STEP

  Phase 1: Counting with meaning, comparing quantities, and the first part-whole ideas, through
  objects and games
  Phase 2: Addition and subtraction as stories, bonds to 10, place value beginnings and the
  teen numbers demystified
  Phase 3: Numbers to 100 and beyond, early measurement, shapes and data, plus problem-solving
  courage and grade-2 readiness

WHAT A STUDENT NEEDS BEFORE STARTING

  Education: Ages 4-7; no academic prerequisites whatsoever
  Math background: None, this course IS the foundation
  Equipment: Computer or tablet with stable internet; everyday objects (blocks, buttons,
    spoons) as materials
  Time commitment: 2 live hours plus everyday math play
  English: Course taught in English
  Parent role: Nearby for the youngest children in early weeks; cheering thereafter

WHO THIS COURSE IS FOR

  First steps: Ages 4-5 taking their very first structured math steps, playfully
  K 2 students: Kindergarten to grade 2 children whose school math needs a stronger foundation
    underneath
  Eager minds: Young children already fascinated by numbers who deserve real food for it
  Worried starts: Children whose first school math experiences created tears, reversible at
    this age, quickly
  Planning parents: Families who want the foundation laid right the first time, before gaps
    exist

FULL CURRICULUM, WEEK BY WEEK

  This is the complete teaching plan. Parents can ask about any week.

  ---------------------------------------------------------------
  PHASE 1: COUNTING THAT MEANS SOMETHING (MONTHS 1-4)
  ---------------------------------------------------------------
  Counting looks simple and hides deep ideas: one number per object, the last number telling
  the total, quantities compared and conserved. This phase builds those ideas properly through
  objects, movement and games, the difference between reciting numbers and understanding them.

    Month 1: Numbers as Quantities (Weeks 1-4)
      A Playful First Look
        Topics:
          - Counting objects to see how far counting flows
          - Comparing two small groups for more or fewer
          - Copying and continuing a simple pattern
          - Noticing how the child talks about numbers
          - Spotting counting habits gently, without correcting
          - Finding a warm, happy starting point
        Practice: Line up a few toys and ask your child to count them and tell you which pile
        has more, keeping it a game and not a test.
        Detail: Playful diagnostic disguised as games: counting, comparing and pattern
        instincts observed
      One Number for Each Thing
        Topics:
          - Touching each object once while saying one number
          - Matching one number word to one thing
          - Understanding the last number tells the total
          - Counting a group and answering how many
          - Recounting a moved group to see the total stays the same
          - Slowing down to count carefully
        Practice: Count the stairs together as you climb, touching each step and cheering the
        final number as the total.
        Detail: One-to-one counting with real objects; the cardinality idea, the last number IS
        the amount
      Seeing Small Numbers Instantly
        Topics:
          - Recognising 1, 2 and 3 without counting
          - Seeing 4 and 5 as quick patterns
          - Reading dice dots at a glance
          - Showing numbers fast with fingers
          - Naming flashed dot cards instantly
          - Talking about how the amount was seen
        Practice: Flash some fingers for a second, hide them, and ask how many your child saw,
        taking turns being the flasher.
        Detail: Subitizing: seeing 3, 4 and 5 without counting, dice, dots and finger patterns
      More, Fewer, or the Same?
        Topics:
          - Comparing two groups for more or fewer
          - Matching items one to one to compare fairly
          - Recognising when two groups are the same
          - Using the words more, fewer and equal
          - Explaining how you know which has more
          - Making two groups equal by adding or taking away
        Practice: Put out two rows of buttons and ask your child to line them up in pairs to
        prove which row has more, or whether they match.
        Detail: Comparing quantities: more, fewer, same, justified with matching, not guessing

    Months 2-3: The Number World to 10 (Weeks 5-12)
      Number Symbols and Counting Both Ways
        Topics:
          - Matching the written numeral to its quantity
          - Recognising the numerals 0 to 10
          - Counting forwards to ten smoothly
          - Counting backwards from ten like a rocket
          - Placing a numeral card beside the right group
          - Writing or tracing numerals playfully
        Practice: Do a rocket countdown from 10 to 0 before a jump or a tickle, then count back
        up to ten together.
        Detail: Numerals connected to quantities; counting forwards and backwards as a game
      The Ten-Frame as Home Base
        Topics:
          - Filling a ten-frame from left to right
          - Seeing a full row of five
          - Reading 7 as five and two more
          - Spotting how many empty spaces are left
          - Seeing numbers hidden inside bigger numbers
          - Knowing how far a number is from ten
        Practice: Draw a two-by-five grid and let your child place counters to show a number
        like 8, then say it as five and three more.
        Detail: Ten-frames as home base: five-and-some structure, seeing numbers inside numbers
      Breaking Numbers into Parts
        Topics:
          - Splitting a small group into two parts
          - Seeing 5 as 2 and 3, or 4 and 1
          - Finding different ways to make the same number
          - Putting the two parts back into the whole
          - Using two hands to hold the two parts
          - Talking about the parts out loud
        Practice: Hide 5 counters behind your back in two hands, show one hand, and let your
        child work out how many are hiding in the other.
        Detail: Part-whole play: 5 is 2-and-3, 4-and-1, decomposition as a toy, years before it
        is a technique
      First, Second, Third and Where Things Sit
        Topics:
          - Using first, second, third and last
          - Describing position with in front, behind and between
          - Walking along a number line as a path
          - Finding which number comes before or after
          - Ordering a small line of toys
          - Naming who is in each place in a line
        Practice: Line up soft toys and ask playful questions like which one is third, or who
        is between the first and the fourth.
        Detail: Ordinal numbers, position words and the number line met as a walking game

    Month 4: Patterns and Sorting + Stage Checkpoint (Weeks 13-16)
      Patterns That Repeat
        Topics:
          - Copying a simple repeating pattern
          - Continuing a pattern by what comes next
          - Creating a brand new pattern of your own
          - Naming the repeating unit, like red blue red blue
          - Spotting patterns in colours, shapes and sounds
          - Fixing a pattern with a deliberate mistake in it
        Practice: Start a pattern with household items, like spoon fork spoon fork, and ask
        what comes next, then let your child build one for you.
        Detail: Repeating patterns: copy, extend, create, the beginnings of algebraic thinking
      Sorting by How Things Are Alike
        Topics:
          - Sorting objects into groups by colour, size or shape
          - Choosing your own rule for sorting
          - Explaining the rule you used
          - Noticing an object that does not belong
          - Sorting the same set a second, different way
          - Describing groups with words like all and none
        Practice: Tip out a box of toys or socks and ask your child to sort them, then guess
        the rule they chose before they tell you.
        Detail: Sorting and classifying by attributes; explaining the rule you sorted by
      Patterns That Grow
        Topics:
          - Seeing a pattern that gets bigger each step
          - Working out what comes next in a growing pattern
          - Building steps like 1, then 2, then 3 blocks
          - Describing how the pattern changes
          - Predicting a later step in the pattern
          - Comparing repeating and growing patterns
        Practice: Build a staircase of blocks that grows by one each time and ask your child
        how many blocks the next step needs.
        Detail: Growing patterns and what-comes-next reasoning
      Phase One Check Through Play
        Topics:
          - Counting a group and telling the total
          - Comparing quantities with more and fewer
          - Showing a number on a ten-frame
          - Copying and extending a pattern
          - Explaining thinking out loud
          - Teaching a skill to a toy or a parent
        Practice: Let your child teach a teddy how to count a small group and spot which pile
        has more, while you happily listen in.
        Assessment: A gentle play-based check of counting, comparing, ten-frames and patterns,
        where the child shows a skill, says how it works, and teaches it to a toy, with no
        pressure.
        Detail: Stage mastery check through play: show it, say it, teach it to your bear

  ---------------------------------------------------------------
  PHASE 2: STORIES, BONDS AND THE TEEN NUMBERS (MONTHS 5-8)
  ---------------------------------------------------------------
  Addition and subtraction arrive as stories acted out with objects, joining, separating,
  comparing, long before symbols carry them. Bonds to 10 grow toward automaticity through
  games, and the famously confusing teen numbers get demystified with place-value materials.

    Month 5: Addition and Subtraction as Stories (Weeks 17-20)
      Adding and Taking Away as Stories
        Topics:
          - Acting out a joining story with objects
          - Acting out a taking-away story
          - Meeting the plus sign as and more
          - Meeting the minus sign as take away
          - Reading a simple number story as a picture
          - Telling the story back in your own words
        Practice: Tell a tiny story with toys, like three ducks and two more join them, and let
        your child act it out and say how many altogether.
        Detail: Joining and separating stories acted with objects; the plus and minus symbols
        as story shorthand
      Counting On and Counting Back
        Topics:
          - Starting from the bigger number and counting on
          - Not going back to one every time
          - Counting back to take away
          - Using fingers to count on a few more
          - Playing the hidden-in-the-hand take-away game
          - Choosing to count on or count back
        Practice: Hold some counters in a closed hand, say the number inside, add a couple on
        top, and let your child count on from the hidden number.
        Detail: Counting on (not starting over) and counting back; the empty-hand subtraction
        game

    Month 6: Bonds of 10 and Fact Families (Weeks 21-24)
      The Pairs That Make Ten
        Topics:
          - Finding two parts that make ten
          - Learning pairs like 6 and 4, 7 and 3
          - Filling a ten-frame to see the missing part
          - Answering the partner of a number quickly
          - Playing many games to make the pairs stick
          - Feeling how ten is a friendly whole
        Practice: Play friends of ten: hold up some fingers on one hand and ask how many more
        make ten, then swap hands.
        Detail: Bonds of 10 through every game we know, the single most valuable fact set in
        mathematics
      One Number Trio, Four Facts
        Topics:
          - Seeing three numbers that belong together
          - Making two addition facts from the trio
          - Making two subtraction facts from the trio
          - Understanding adding and taking away as linked
          - Using one known fact to find the others
          - Building the whole fact family from a picture
        Practice: Give your child three numbers like 2, 8 and 10 and see how many facts they
        can say using all three.
        Detail: Fact families: 3+7, 7+3, 10-7, 10-3 as one idea seen four ways

    Month 7: Teen Numbers and Place Value Beginnings (Weeks 25-28)
      Teen Numbers Are Ten and Some More
        Topics:
          - Building a teen number as one ten and some ones
          - Seeing 14 as ten and four
          - Grouping ten small items into one bundle
          - Reading teen numbers correctly
          - Understanding where place value begins
          - Matching the numeral to the ten-and-ones picture
        Practice: Bundle ten straws or sticks with a band, add a few loose ones, and ask your
        child to name the teen number you made.
        Detail: Teens demystified: 14 as ten-and-four, built with materials, where place value
        actually starts
      All the Way to Twenty
        Topics:
          - Counting forwards and backwards to 20
          - Comparing two numbers up to 20
          - Ordering numbers up to 20
          - Filling a second ten-frame past ten
          - Previewing the make-ten bridge as a game
          - Spotting the ten inside a teen number
        Practice: Count a bigger pile of objects, like 16 pasta pieces, into two ten-frames,
        then ask which of two numbers up to 20 is bigger.
        Detail: Numbers to 20: counting, comparing, and bridging-through-10 previewed as a game

    Month 8: Story Problems and the Explain Habit (Weeks 29-32)
      Act It, Draw It, Write It
        Topics:
          - Acting out a word problem with objects
          - Drawing a simple picture of the story
          - Writing the matching number sentence
          - Finding the question hidden in the story
          - Deciding whether to join or take away
          - Checking the answer against the story
        Practice: Make up a little story, such as five apples and two eaten, and guide your
        child to act it, draw it, then write the number sentence.
        Detail: Word problems as theatre: act it, draw it, then write it, the three-step that
        prevents future word-problem fear
      Missing Numbers and Phase Two Check
        Topics:
          - Finding a missing number in a simple sentence
          - Thinking backwards from an answer
          - Using fact families to fill the gap
          - Reviewing story problems and bonds of ten
          - Explaining how a puzzle was solved
          - Showing teen numbers as ten and ones
        Practice: Pose a gentle puzzle like something plus 3 makes 7 using counters, and let
        your child find the missing amount.
        Assessment: A relaxed play-based check of story problems, bonds of ten, fact families
        and teen numbers, where the child solves a puzzle and explains the thinking, with no
        pressure.
        Detail: Missing-number puzzles and both-ways thinking; stage mastery check through play

  ---------------------------------------------------------------
  PHASE 3: TO 100 AND INTO THE WORLD (MONTHS 9-12)
  ---------------------------------------------------------------
  The number world expands to 100 with place-value understanding, and math steps into the
  child's world: measuring, money, time, shapes and simple data. The course closes with
  problem-solving courage and a confident handoff to grade-level mathematics.

    Month 9: The Road to 100 (Weeks 33-36)
      Building Numbers from Tens and Ones
        Topics:
          - Building a two-digit number from tens and ones
          - Bundling tens and counting the leftover ones
          - Reading a number like 34 as three tens and four
          - Comparing two two-digit numbers
          - Ordering several numbers from small to big
          - Matching the numeral to the tens-and-ones model
        Practice: Use grouped straws or blocks to build a number like 27, then build another
        and ask your child which is bigger and why.
        Detail: Tens and ones with materials: building two-digit numbers, comparing and
        ordering them
      Skip Counting and the Hundred Square
        Topics:
          - Skip counting by 10s to one hundred
          - Skip counting by 5s and by 2s
          - Hearing skip counting as a rhythm
          - Finding patterns on the hundred square
          - Moving up, down and across the hundred square
          - Spotting the tens column and its counting patterns
        Practice: Chant counting by tens up to a hundred on a walk, then try by fives, clapping
        to keep the rhythm.
        Detail: Skip counting by 2s, 5s and 10s as rhythm and pattern; the 100-square explored
        like a map

    Month 10: Two-Digit Confidence (Weeks 37-40)
      Adding Two-Digit Numbers
        Topics:
          - Adding two numbers using tens and ones blocks
          - Combining the tens, then the ones
          - Moving from blocks to picturing the jump
          - Adding a whole ten to a number
          - Solving sums like 23 plus 14
          - Checking the answer with the materials
        Practice: Set out blocks for a sum like 22 plus 13 and let your child join the tens and
        the ones, then say the total.
        Detail: Adding tens, adding ones: two-digit addition with materials first, mental jumps
        second
      Ten More and Ten Less
        Topics:
          - Finding ten more than a number quickly
          - Finding ten less than a number
          - Using the hundred square to jump by ten
          - Noticing only the tens digit changes
          - Meeting friendly round numbers
          - Jumping to the next friendly ten
        Practice: Say a number like 34 and ask for ten more, then ten less, using the hundred
        square to check each jump.
        Detail: Ten-more ten-less fluency; friendly-number thinking previewed gently

    Month 11: Measurement, Money and Time (Weeks 41-44)
      Measuring and Guessing
        Topics:
          - Comparing lengths as longer and shorter
          - Comparing weights as heavier and lighter
          - Comparing capacity as holds more or less
          - Measuring with repeated units like paper clips
          - Guessing a measurement, then checking it
          - Using words like longest, heaviest and full
        Practice: Guess how many hand-spans long the table is, then measure together to see how
        close the guess was.
        Detail: Length, weight and capacity by comparing and then by counting units; estimation
        as a guessing game with feedback
      Money and Telling the Time
        Topics:
          - Recognising a few common coins
          - Paying for small pretend items
          - Counting a small amount of money
          - Reading o'clock on a real clock
          - Reading half-past on a real clock
          - Linking times to parts of the day
        Practice: Play shop with real coins for a few priced items, then check what o'clock it
        is on a real clock together.
        Detail: Coins and simple shopping play; o'clock and half-past on real clocks

    Month 12: Shapes, Data and Graduation (Weeks 45-52)
      Shapes and Fair Shares
        Topics:
          - Naming flat shapes like circle, square and triangle
          - Naming solid shapes like cube, sphere and cone
          - Building and hunting for shapes at home
          - Describing shapes by their sides and corners
          - Sharing something fairly into halves
          - Sharing into quarters as four equal parts
        Practice: Go on a shape hunt around the house, then share a snack or a drawing fairly
        into halves and quarters.
        Detail: 2D and 3D shapes built, named and hunted at home; halves and quarters as fair
        sharing, fractions met kindly
      Graphs, Graduation and the Road Ahead
        Topics:
          - Asking a simple survey question
          - Collecting answers from family or class
          - Drawing a picture graph of the results
          - Reading which answer had the most
          - Teaching a favourite math game to others
          - Looking ahead to grade-level math
        Practice: Help your child survey the family on a fun question, like favourite fruit,
        and draw a little picture graph of the answers.
        Assessment: A gentle final celebration where the child makes a simple pictograph,
        teaches a favourite math game, and revisits the year's ideas, with a friendly
        road-ahead plan instead of a test.
        Detail: Simple pictographs from the child's own surveys; graduation project, the child
        teaches their favourite math game, and the road-ahead plan into grade-level math

COMMON QUESTIONS ABOUT THIS COURSE

  For anything about cost, use PART 4 and RULE 1. Do not quote two regions.

  Q: Can a 4-year-old really learn in online classes?
  A: Yes, with the right design, which is the whole craft here. Classes run as short, varied
  playful segments: a counting game, a building challenge, a story problem, a movement break
  with skip counting. The mentor works with real objects the child holds up to the camera, and
  parents of our youngest students sit nearby for the first weeks. The free demo shows you
  exactly how it works with your child. (Agent note: the free demo is a waiting list with no
  fixed date. The Priority Live Demo is a guaranteed class today or tomorrow, booked at
  https://learn.modernagecoders.com/priority-demo . Offer both, as RULE 3 says.)

  Q: Isn't this age too early for structured math?
  A: It is exactly the right age for the right kind: playful, concrete, talk-rich mathematics.
  Research on early number sense is unambiguous, the part-whole and counting ideas built at 4-7
  predict mathematics success for years. What would be wrong at this age is worksheets and
  drilling, which is why we do neither.

  Q: How is this different from apps like Khan Kids or busy-work workbooks?
  A: Apps entertain and practice; they cannot listen. The engine of early math learning is math
  talk, a child explaining 'I saw 5 because 4-and-1' to a person who responds. Our mentors have
  that conversation twice a week, notice exactly which ideas have landed, and adjust in real
  time. No app does that.

  Q: My child already loves numbers. Will this stretch them?
  A: Happily, the mentor teaches to stage, not age. A number-loving five-year-old might race
  into part-whole play and early place value while a classmate consolidates counting. Small
  groups and 1-on-1 make that flexibility real.

  Q: What do parents need to do at home?
  A: Kitchens and car rides teach more early math than worksheets ever did, and we show you how
  to use them.

  Q: What comes after this course?
  A: Graduates flow into Mental Maths Mastery (for fluency depth) or the Elementary Mathematics
  Masterclass (the full grades 1-5 program) with the same mentor where possible, arriving with
  the foundation those courses quietly assume.

  Q: How is my child assessed, and is the certificate just for attending?
  A: No. A problem set follows every class with written feedback, monthly reviews deliberately
  mix new material with earlier topics so nothing is forgotten, and the course ends with a
  final assessment (a friendly, low-pressure check of the whole year). Passing earns the
  certificate; falling short earns focused revision and a free retest. We measure real
  understanding, not attendance.

  Q: Can we try it before paying?
  A: Yes. Every child starts with a free live demo class that doubles as the playful
  diagnostic, no card details, no obligation, and you will know within the hour whether your
  child lights up.

WHAT THIS COURSE IS

  Elementary maths classes for Grades 1-5, live and online: placement by grade into three
  school-year levels, from counting to fractions, geometry and pre-algebra.

  In one line: Three honest school-year levels instead of one endless course: your child is placed where they are, and finishes each level actually owning it.

ABOUT THE PROGRAMME

  Primary maths is where number confidence is either built or broken, and it cannot be rushed.
  That is why this program is structured the way good schools structure it: three levels, each
  one school year long. Level A builds Grades 1-2: counting, place value, addition and
  subtraction, shapes, time and money. Level B builds Grades 3-4: multiplication and division
  fluency, fractions, decimals, data and real geometry. Level C completes Grade 5 and builds
  the bridge to middle school: advanced fractions, ratios, percentages, circle geometry, first
  algebra and probability. Every child starts with a short, friendly placement check and joins
  the level that fits, never the one their age assumes. Classes are live and small, and the
  method is the one the strongest primary curricula in the world use: concrete first (objects
  and drawings), then pictorial, then abstract. Practice is 20 to 30 minutes daily rather than
  marathon sessions, because at this age consistency beats intensity every single time. Each
  level runs 10 months of teaching at two live classes a week, with up to 12 months for
  children who need more repetition, the pace adapts, never the standard. Learning is checked
  the honest way: homework after every class, weekly mixed practice that deliberately revisits
  earlier topics, a mid-level check, and a level exam at the end. Passing earns the level
  certificate and promotion; a child who falls short gets focused revision and a free retest.
  Real knowledge, real work, depth over dopamine.

WHAT MAKES THIS COURSE DIFFERENT

  - Placement by level, not by age: a short friendly check decides where your child starts, so
    nothing is skipped and nothing is repeated
  - Concrete, pictorial, abstract: every concept starts with objects and pictures before symbols,
    the sequence the world's best primary curricula use
  - Spiral revision is built in: weekly practice deliberately mixes older topics with new ones,
    so skills stop fading between terms
  - 20-30 minutes of daily practice, not marathon sessions: at this age consistency beats
    intensity
  - Real assessment, gently done: a mid-level check and a level exam decide the certificate, with
    focused revision and a free retest when needed
  - Parents stay in the loop: regular written notes on what was learned, what is next, and
    exactly how to help at home

THE LEARNING PATH, STEP BY STEP

  Phase 1: Level A, Grades 1-2 (one school year): counting and place value, addition and
  subtraction, first multiplication, shapes, time, money and measurement
  Phase 2: Level B, Grades 3-4 (one school year): multiplication and division fluency,
  fractions, decimals, data and graphing, geometry, area and perimeter
  Phase 3: Level C, Grade 5 (one school year): large numbers, advanced fractions, ratios and
  percentages, circle geometry, first algebra, probability and money maths

WHAT A STUDENT NEEDS BEFORE STARTING

  Reading: Basic reading helps from Grade 2 up; Level A supports early readers with visual

  Equipment: A computer or tablet with a stable internet connection; a notebook and pencil
    matter more than any app
  Age: Grades 1-5 (roughly ages 6-11). Placement is by a short friendly check, never age alone
  Time commitment: 2 live classes plus 20-30 minutes of practice a day

  Moving ahead: Confident children who finish school worksheets early and are hungry for more

COMMON QUESTIONS ABOUT THIS COURSE

  For anything about cost, use PART 4 and RULE 1. Do not quote two regions.

  Q: Which level will my child join?
  A: A short, friendly placement check decides, never age alone. Level A builds Grades 1-2
  (counting to first multiplication, time, money), Level B builds Grades 3-4 (multiplication
  and division fluency, fractions, decimals, geometry), and Level C completes Grade 5 (ratios,
  percentages, first algebra, probability). Most children join the level matching their grade;
  children with gaps start where the gaps are, because skipping holes in maths only buries
  them.

  Q: How long does each level take?
  A: Each level is one school year: 10 months of teaching at 2 live classes a week, with up to
  12 months for children who need more repetition. That margin is deliberate, at this age the
  pace adapts to the child, never the other way around. A child who starts in Level A and
  continues through Level C finishes elementary maths genuinely owned, not skimmed.

  Q: How is my child assessed? Is the certificate just for attending?
  A: No. There is classwork in every session, a short homework sheet after every class, weekly
  mixed practice that deliberately revisits earlier topics, a friendly quiz at each month-pair,
  a mid-level check, and a level exam at the end: a written paper plus a short viva. Passing
  earns the level certificate and promotion; a child who falls short gets focused revision and
  a free retest. Gentle in tone, real in standard.

  Q: My child struggles with maths anxiety. How does this course help?
  A: By removing the two causes: gaps and pace. Placement starts the child where their gaps
  actually are, and every concept begins with objects and pictures before symbols, so
  understanding always precedes speed. Classes are small, wins are celebrated, and practice is
  20 to 30 minutes daily rather than exhausting marathons. Most anxious children change their
  mind about maths within one level, because the anxiety was never about maths, it was about
  being lost.

  Q: How is this different from school tuition?
  A: Tuition usually chases this week's homework. This is a complete levelled curriculum with
  its own arc: placement, spiral revision, monthly checks and a level exam, so gaps get found
  and closed instead of papered over. It runs alongside any school board comfortably, CBSE,
  ICSE or international, because Grades 1-5 maths is the same mathematics everywhere.

  Q: How much time does it take each week?
  A: Two live classes a week plus 20 to 30 minutes of daily practice, usually structured as
  games and short challenge sets. At this age consistency beats intensity: twenty focused daily
  minutes outperform a two-hour weekend session every time, and it never becomes a fight at the
  kitchen table.

  Q: Will this prepare my child for olympiads?
  A: It builds the foundation olympiads stand on: real fluency, flexible problem solving and
  comfort with multi-step reasoning. Level C includes genuine puzzle work. Children who love
  that side graduate naturally into our dedicated olympiad mathematics courses, which train
  competition technique specifically.

  no fixed date. The Priority Live Demo is a guaranteed class today or tomorrow, booked at

  Q: Are classes live or recorded?
  A: Every class is live: a small group with a real teacher who sees your child's working in
  real time, never a pre-recorded video. At this age the teacher's eyes matter most, catching
  the finger-counting, the reversed digits, the guess dressed as an answer, and fixing each
  gently before it becomes a habit.

WHAT THIS COURSE IS

  Ethical hacking and cybersecurity course for adults: networking and Linux, authorized
  penetration testing, web and network exploitation, red and blue team skills, and professional
  reporting, taught legally and ethically, in 10-12 months.

  In one line: Break in so you can defend: authorized penetration testing taught the professional way, from networking and Linux to red team operations and reports that get vulnerabilities fixed.

ABOUT THE PROGRAMME

  Ethical hacking is authorized, legal security testing done to find and fix weaknesses before
  criminals do, and the emphasis in this course is on the word ethical. It is built for people
  who want a real cybersecurity career, penetration tester, security analyst, red or blue team
  engineer, and it starts every offensive skill from a foundation of authorization, scope and
  law. The path is complete and in order: networking, Linux and programming for security,
  reconnaissance and scanning, then core exploitation, web and network attacks, Metasploit, the
  OWASP Top 10, post-exploitation, all practised only in lab environments and authorized
  ranges, then advanced work: buffer overflows and mitigation bypasses, cryptography, red team
  operations, and the defensive side, DevSecOps, threat hunting, incident response and
  forensics, so you understand both attack and defence. A finale month runs a full authorized
  penetration test of a lab and writes the professional report, then sits the final exam. The
  pace is honest: ten teaching months at two live classes a week plus four to six hours of lab
  practice, with two more in hand. Problem sets, monthly mixed reviews, phase exams, and a
  final exam that decides the certificate with a free retest.

WHAT MAKES THIS COURSE DIFFERENT

  - Ethics and authorization first, not as a footnote: scope, consent and law frame every
    technique
  - Everything practised in labs and authorized ranges only, never against systems you do not own
  - Both sides taught: offensive skills and the defensive DevSecOps, threat-hunting and forensics
    response
  - Professional reporting is a core skill: findings that actually get fixed, not just exploits
  - An honest 10-month arc with 2 months in hand
  - Real assessment: weekly problem sets, monthly mixed reviews, phase exams and a final exam
    with a free retest

THE LEARNING PATH, STEP BY STEP

  Phase 1: Foundations and recon (Months 1-3): networking, Linux, programming, ethics, OSINT
  and scanning
  Phase 2: Core exploitation (Months 4-6): system, web and network attacks, post-exploitation,
  advanced domains
  Phase 3: Advanced and defensive (Months 7-9): exploit development, red team, DevSecOps,

  - Phase 2: exploitation, web-attack and post-exploitation labs, all in controlled environments
  - Phase 3: exploit-development, red-team and blue-team defensive labs
  - Phase 4: the full authorized lab pentest and its professional report

  Total projects: 20+ lab-based engagements, crowned by a full authorized penetration test and report

SKILLS THE STUDENT WILL HAVE AT THE END

  - The legal and ethical foundation: authorization, scope, disclosure and law

  - Advanced offensive: exploit development, mitigation bypasses, red team operations
  - Defensive security: DevSecOps, threat hunting, incident response and forensics
  - Professional penetration-test reporting

HOW A TYPICAL WEEK IS SPLIT

  Live classes: 2 live one-hour classes per week, coding along with the instructor
  Homework: A problem set after every class, and a mixed-review assignment at the end of every
    month
  Practice: 4-6 hours of building between classes
  Review: Every submission reviewed with written feedback; recurring gaps reopened in class

SUPPORT INCLUDED

  Doubt support: WhatsApp doubt support between classes
  Progress updates: Honest monthly progress reviews: what is solid, what is wobbly, and the
    plan for the wobble

CERTIFICATION DETAIL

  Completion: Certificate from Modern Age Coders, awarded on passing the final exam. Fall short
    and there is focused revision and a free retest: the certificate certifies knowledge, not
    attendance

WHERE THIS CAN LEAD

  - Penetration tester, security analyst and red or blue team roles
  - Certifications: this course prepares the ground for CEH and OSCP
  - Specializations: web, cloud, mobile or ICS security
  - Defensive tracks: SOC, threat hunting and incident response

  environments and authorized ranges we provide.

  career-changers and IT professionals.

COMMON QUESTIONS ABOUT THIS COURSE

  For anything about cost, use PART 4 and RULE 1. Do not quote two regions.

  Q: What does this Flutter course cover?
  A: Dart as a real language first, then Flutter properly: the widget mental model, layouts and
  navigation that feel native on both platforms, state management chosen with judgment,
  architecture that survives features, Firebase auth and data, offline behavior, testing and
  release discipline. A finale month ships a capstone app verified on Android and iOS and sits
  the final exam.

  Q: How long does it take to learn Flutter properly?
  A: Ten months of teaching at 2 live classes a week plus 4 to 6 hours of practice, with two
  more months in hand for learners who need them. The three teaching phases build the skill and
  its real-world application; the finale month ships a capstone and sits the final exam.

  Q: How am I assessed? Is the certificate just for attending?
  A: No. Problem sets follow every class with written feedback, monthly reviews deliberately
  mix new material with earlier topics, each phase ends with a cumulative exam, and the course
  ends with a final exam: a practical build plus written questions from the whole syllabus.
  Passing earns the certificate; falling short earns focused revision and a free retest.

  Q: Flutter or React Native?
  A: Both are honest cross-platform answers. Flutter wins on UI consistency and
  performance-by-default with one language (Dart); React Native wins for teams already deep in
  JavaScript. We teach both roads in different courses; this one is the Flutter road, chosen
  most by builders who want pixel-level control on both platforms.

  Q: Do I need a Mac for this course?
  A: Not for learning: Android covers the entire journey on any computer, and the iOS build
  step is taught honestly as a release-time requirement (Apple mandates a Mac there). Students
  shipping to the App Store later use a borrowed, used or cloud Mac at that point, stated
  upfront rather than discovered late.

  Q: Can I try a class before enrolling?
  A: Yes, a free demo class with no commitment: book at learn.modernagecoders.com/contact or
  message us on WhatsApp at +91 91233 66161. (Agent note: the free demo is a waiting list with
  no fixed date. The Priority Live Demo is a guaranteed class today or tomorrow, booked at
  https://learn.modernagecoders.com/priority-demo . Offer both, as RULE 3 says.)

  Q: Are classes live or recorded?
  A: Live, always: small groups with a real instructor reading your actual code, never
  pre-recorded videos.
