Course link: https://learn.modernagecoders.com/courses/jee-foundation-maths-course-class-8-10
Subject area: Foundation Mathematics
Designed for: High school
Who can join: Class 8 to 10 students, batched by class
Course length: 12 months (48 weeks)
Time needed: 2 live classes/week + 3-4 hours of problem sets
Certificate: Certificate from Modern Age Coders, awarded on passing the final assessment

PRICE FOR THIS COURSE (quote only the one that applies to the person asking)
  In India, per month:      group Rs 1,499, mini batch Rs 2,999, one to one Rs 4,999
  Outside India, per month: group $100, one to one $150
  Classes: group and mini batch two live classes a week, eight a month; one to one in India one
  live class a week, four a month; one to one outside India two live classes a week, eight a
  month. Each class is one hour.

WHAT THIS COURSE IS

  JEE foundation maths course for Class 8-10: NCERT-aligned depth, geometry proof skills,
  olympiad-style problem solving and timed MCQ practice in live batches.

  In one line: Class 11 physics and maths punish shaky algebra. This course is where the algebra stops being shaky.

ABOUT THE PROGRAMME

  Most students who struggle in JEE preparation do not struggle with Class 11 topics; they
  struggle with Class 8 to 10 topics that were never made solid. Fractions handled nervously,
  identities half-remembered, geometry never actually proved. A foundation course exists to fix
  that before it costs anything, and this one does it honestly: no rank promises, no 'future
  IITian' theatre, just the school syllabus taught deeper than school goes, plus the
  problem-solving habits that entrance exams eventually demand. The 12-month plan runs in four
  phases. First, numbers and algebra at real depth: divisibility and remainders, exponents and
  surds, identities and factorisation, equations and inequalities. Second, geometry as a proof
  discipline, congruence, similarity, circles, because writing a correct proof is the closest a
  school student comes to real mathematical thinking. Third, mensuration, introductory
  trigonometry and coordinate geometry, the toolkit chapters. Fourth, the part school never
  teaches: problem-solving heuristics, olympiad-style questions, and a full timed MCQ phase in
  the style of NTSE-type talent exams and entrance papers, with error logs and review clinics.
  Content is NCERT-aligned and batched by class, so a Class 8 student and a Class 10 student
  meet the same ideas at different depths. School marks tend to improve as a side effect; the
  actual product is a student who reaches Class 11 with nothing to repair.

WHAT MAKES THIS COURSE DIFFERENT

  - NCERT-aligned but deeper: every chapter is taken past the textbook stopping point, into the
    why and the harder problem forms
  - Proof skills taught deliberately: given, to prove, construction, proof, drilled until writing
    a geometry argument feels normal
  - A genuine problem-solving phase: heuristics like working backwards, small cases and clean
    diagrams, practised on olympiad-style questions
  - A full timed MCQ phase with error logs: elimination, option testing and time budgeting, the
    craft entrance exams actually test
  - Honest positioning: this is foundation, not JEE coaching, and we say plainly that nobody can
    promise selections or ranks
  - Batched by class: Class 8, 9 and 10 groups meet the same arc at the right depth, so nobody is
    drowned or bored

THE LEARNING PATH, STEP BY STEP

  Phase 1: Numbers and algebra at depth: divisibility and remainders, exponents and surds,
  identities, factorisation, equations and inequalities
  Phase 2: Geometry as a proof discipline: angles, congruence, similarity, quadrilaterals and
  circle theorems, with proof writing drilled throughout
  Phase 3: The toolkit chapters: mensuration in 2D and 3D, introductory trigonometry with
  heights and distances, and coordinate geometry
  Phase 4: Problem-solving heuristics and olympiad-style questions, then a timed MCQ and mock
  phase with error clinics and a readiness review

WHAT A STUDENT NEEDS BEFORE STARTING

  Maths level: Comfortable with the previous class's school maths. The week 1 diagnostic finds
    the gaps and the early weeks patch them
  Class: Class 8, 9 or 10. Batches are separated by class so depth and pace fit the student
  Equipment: The student's NCERT maths textbook, a geometry box, graph paper, notebooks, and a
    device with stable internet
  Mindset: Willingness to write solutions out in full. This course grades reasoning, not just
    answers

WHO THIS COURSE IS FOR

  Future jee aspirants: Students in Class 8 to 10 who intend to attempt JEE or similar
    entrances and want the base built before Class 11 raises the stakes
  Strong students underfed: Students who find school maths easy and are bored, and need harder
    problems rather than more of the same
  Proof never taught: Students who can compute but have never been taught to prove, which is
    most students
  Mcq first timers: Students who have only ever written school papers and need timed MCQ craft
    before any talent or entrance exam
  Families avoiding hype: Parents who want serious foundation work without rank promises and
    future-topper theatre

FULL CURRICULUM, WEEK BY WEEK

  This is the complete teaching plan. Parents can ask about any week.

  ---------------------------------------------------------------
  PHASE 1: NUMBERS AND ALGEBRA AT DEPTH (MONTHS 1-3, WEEKS 1-12)
  ---------------------------------------------------------------
  The chapters every entrance exam quietly assumes: number theory basics, exponents and surds,
  identities, factorisation, and equations, taken well past the textbook stopping point.

    Month 1: Number Systems, Properly (Weeks 1-4)
      Weeks 1-2: The Number Line, End to End
        Topics:
          - Diagnostic paper: arithmetic, fractions, basic algebra and geometry from earlier classes
          - Integers, rationals and irrationals, and how to prove a number belongs where it does
          - Decimal expansions: terminating, recurring, and converting recurring decimals to fractions
          - Representing surds on the number line
          - Density: finding rationals and irrationals between any two numbers
          - Comparing numbers cleverly: without calculators, by squaring or bounding
        Projects built:
          - Number-line dossier: one page classifying 20 assorted numbers with a one-line justification
            each
        Practice: 30 classification and conversion problems, including 5 recurring-decimal
        conversions written out in full
      Weeks 3-4: Divisibility and Remainders
        Topics:
          - Divisibility rules for 2 through 11, proved rather than just stated
          - Primes, composites and prime factorisation as the master tool
          - HCF and LCM: computation, the product relationship, and word problems
          - Remainder thinking: what is left when powers are divided, kept concrete
          - Digit problems: unit digits of large powers, digit sums
          - First olympiad-style flavour: divisibility puzzles with small numbers
        Projects built:
          - Divisibility rule proof sheet: the rules for 3, 9 and 11 explained in the student's own words
            with examples
        Practice: 25 divisibility and HCF-LCM problems plus 5 unit-digit puzzles, hardest two
        attempted before class discussion
        Assessment: Month 1 test: a 25-mark paper on number systems mixing standard questions
        with two puzzle-style problems

    Month 2: Exponents, Surds and Identities (Weeks 5-8)
      Weeks 5-6: Exponents and Surds
        Topics:
          - Laws of exponents for integer and rational powers, with the proofs sketched
          - Negative and fractional exponents handled without fear
          - Surds: simplifying, adding, and rationalising denominators including two-term denominators
          - Comparing surds and exponential expressions by clever bounding
          - Scientific notation and orders of magnitude
          - Exam forms: simplify-this-monster questions and how to dismantle them
        Projects built:
          - Simplification gauntlet: 10 layered exponent-surd expressions reduced step by step, each step
            justified
        Practice: 35 exponent and surd problems including 8 rationalisations and 5 comparison
        questions without a calculator
      Weeks 7-8: Identities and Factorisation
        Topics:
          - The square and cube identities, derived, visualised, and drilled
          - Sum and difference of cubes, and the three-variable identity for a cubed sum
          - Factorisation strategy: common factors, grouping, splitting the middle term, identities
          - The remainder theorem and factor theorem, introduced with numeric checks
          - Evaluating expressions cleverly: 99 squared, 101 cubed via identities
          - Identity-based olympiad-style problems: finding values without finding variables
        Projects built:
          - Identity map: every identity in the phase on one sheet with a numeric example and one exam
            use each
        Practice: 30 factorisations across all five strategies plus 8 evaluate-cleverly
        problems, strategy named before each
        Assessment: Month 2 test: a 30-mark paper on exponents, surds and identities including
        two multi-step simplifications

    Month 3: Equations and Inequalities (Weeks 9-12)
      Weeks 9-10: Linear Equations and Systems
        Topics:
          - Linear equations in one variable, including fractional and bracketed forms
          - Word-problem craft: translating ages, digits, mixtures and motion into equations
          - Pairs of linear equations: substitution and elimination done cleanly
          - Consistency: when systems have one, many or no solutions, seen graphically
          - Parameter questions: for what value of k does the system break
          - Checking solutions as a habit, not an afterthought
        Projects built:
          - Translation drill sheet: 12 word problems converted to equations before any are solved
        Practice: 25 equations and systems plus 8 word problems, with the check step written
        for every answer
      Weeks 11-12: Inequalities and a First Look at Quadratics
        Topics:
          - Linear inequalities: solving, representing on the number line, and the sign-flip rule proved
          - Compound conditions: and versus or, read carefully
          - Quadratic equations by factorisation: the bridge from identities to solving
          - The idea of a discriminant, previewed for the Class 10 batch
          - Absolute value as distance, kept geometric and gentle
          - Phase consolidation: mixed algebra sets that do not announce their chapter
        Projects built:
          - Personal error log opened: every phase 1 test miss classified as concept, method or slip,
            used all year
        Practice: 20 inequalities and 15 factorisation-solved quadratics, plus one mixed set of
        15 unannounced problems
        Assessment: Phase 1 milestone: a 40-mark numbers-and-algebra paper, one third of it in
        MCQ format as a preview of phase 4

  ---------------------------------------------------------------
  PHASE 2: GEOMETRY AS A PROOF DISCIPLINE (MONTHS 4-6, WEEKS 13-24)
  ---------------------------------------------------------------
  Geometry is where students first learn what mathematical certainty means. Congruence,
  similarity, quadrilaterals and circles, with proof writing drilled from the first week.

    Month 4: Angles, Triangles and Congruence (Weeks 13-16)
      Weeks 13-14: Lines, Angles and What a Proof Is
        Topics:
          - Angles on a line, vertically opposite angles, and angles with parallel lines
          - The triangle angle-sum result and exterior angle theorem, proved
          - What a proof is: statements, reasons, and why 'it looks true' is not enough
          - The four-part format: given, to prove, construction, proof
          - Angle chasing: finding unknown angles in layered figures
          - Drawing honest figures: large, labelled, and not misleadingly special
        Projects built:
          - First proof portfolio entries: angle-sum and exterior-angle proofs written in full four-part
            format
        Practice: 20 angle-chasing figures of rising difficulty plus 2 proofs, every figure
        redrawn by hand before solving
      Weeks 15-16: Congruence
        Topics:
          - Congruence criteria: SAS, ASA, AAS, SSS and RHS, and why AAA fails
          - Choosing the right criterion: reading the figure for what is actually given
          - Isosceles triangle results, proved both directions
          - Inequalities in a triangle: bigger side, bigger angle, and the triangle inequality
          - Multi-step congruence proofs: proving parts equal via congruent triangles
          - Common proof errors: assuming the conclusion, circular reasoning, unstated steps
        Projects built:
          - Criterion sorting sheet: 12 figures matched to their congruence criterion with the given
            parts marked
        Practice: 15 congruence problems including 5 full proofs, each proof peer-checked
        against the four-part format
        Assessment: Month 4 test: a 25-mark geometry paper with two full proofs marked strictly
        on structure and justification

    Month 5: Similarity, Pythagoras and Quadrilaterals (Weeks 17-20)
      Weeks 17-18: Similarity and Pythagoras
        Topics:
          - Similar triangles: the AA, SSS and SAS similarity criteria
          - The basic proportionality theorem and its converse
          - How similarity scales lengths and areas differently, seen with numbers first
          - The Pythagoras theorem proved by similarity, and its converse
          - Applications: heights via shadows, distances across rivers, ladders and slopes
          - Pythagorean triples and spotting them fast in MCQs
        Projects built:
          - Proof portfolio extended: BPT and the similarity proof of Pythagoras written in full
        Practice: 20 similarity and Pythagoras problems including 3 proofs and 5 real-setting
        applications
      Weeks 19-20: Quadrilaterals and the Midpoint Theorem
        Topics:
          - The parallelogram theorems: sides, angles and diagonals, proved and reversed
          - Tests for a parallelogram: which minimal facts force the shape
          - Rectangle, rhombus and square as parallelograms with extra conditions
          - The midpoint theorem and its converse, with applications
          - Multi-step figures: midpoints inside triangles inside parallelograms
          - Proof strategy: what to construct when the figure refuses to yield
        Projects built:
          - Quadrilateral family tree: the shapes and the exact conditions separating them, made by the
            student
        Practice: 18 quadrilateral problems including 4 proofs, plus 5 midpoint-theorem
        applications
        Assessment: Month 5 test: a 25-mark paper on similarity and quadrilaterals with two
        proofs and one construction-strategy question

    Month 6: Circles and the Geometry Workshop (Weeks 21-24)
      Weeks 21-22: Circle Theorems
        Topics:
          - Chords: equal chords, distances from the centre, the perpendicular from the centre
          - The central angle theorem: the angle at the centre doubles the angle at the arc
          - Angles in the same segment, and the angle in a semicircle
          - Cyclic quadrilaterals and their opposite angles
          - Tangents: perpendicularity to the radius and equal tangents from an external point
          - Angle chasing in circle figures, the entrance-exam favourite
        Projects built:
          - Circle theorem atlas: every theorem drawn, stated and proved or justified on the student's
            own pages
        Practice: 20 circle problems from single-theorem to three-theorem figures, plus 2 full
        proofs
      Weeks 23-24: The Geometry Problem Workshop
        Topics:
          - Hard multi-step figures mixing congruence, similarity, quadrilaterals and circles
          - Auxiliary constructions: when and what to draw, taught as a decision, not magic
          - Working backwards from what must be proved
          - Olympiad-style geometry: problems where the figure is the puzzle
          - Timed geometry MCQs: answering from the figure without full proofs
          - Phase review: the proof portfolio completed and audited
        Projects built:
          - Workshop set: 6 multi-step geometry problems solved with the construction decision written
            out for each
        Practice: One timed 15-question geometry MCQ set plus 4 workshop problems, error log
        updated with figure-reading misses
        Assessment: Phase 2 milestone: a 40-mark geometry paper, half proofs and half timed
        MCQs, with a one-on-one proof review

  ---------------------------------------------------------------
  PHASE 3: MENSURATION, TRIGONOMETRY AND COORDINATES (MONTHS 7-9, WEEKS 25-36)
  ---------------------------------------------------------------
  The toolkit chapters every entrance exam draws on: 2D and 3D mensuration, introductory
  trigonometry with heights and distances, and coordinate geometry.

    Month 7: Mensuration in Two and Three Dimensions (Weeks 25-28)
      Weeks 25-26: Areas in the Plane
        Topics:
          - Areas of triangles: half base times height, and Heron's formula for when heights hide
          - Areas of parallelograms, trapeziums and rhombuses, derived not memorised
          - Circles, sectors and segments, with arc lengths
          - Composite figures: decomposing shaded regions cleanly
          - Same base, same parallels: area relationships without any measuring
          - Estimation checks: is that area plausible for that figure
        Projects built:
          - Decomposition sheet: 8 shaded-region problems with the cut lines drawn and named before any
            formula is used
        Practice: 22 area problems including 5 Heron applications and 5 composite figures,
        decomposition stated in one line each
      Weeks 27-28: Solids and Scaling
        Topics:
          - Surface areas and volumes: cube, cuboid, cylinder, cone, sphere, hemisphere
          - Combined solids and which surfaces vanish at the joins
          - Melting and recasting problems: volume as the conserved quantity
          - Scaling laws: double the length, four times the area, eight times the volume
          - Unit discipline across centimetres, metres and litres
          - MCQ forms: ratio-based mensuration questions solved without computing either quantity
        Projects built:
          - Scaling experiment write-up: one solid scaled by 2 and by 3, with areas and volumes tabulated
            and the pattern stated
        Practice: 18 solid problems including 4 recasting and 4 ratio questions, units checked
        on every line
        Assessment: Month 7 test: a 25-mark mensuration paper mixing computation, ratio
        reasoning and one composite figure

    Month 8: Introductory Trigonometry (Weeks 29-32)
      Weeks 29-30: Ratios and Identities
        Topics:
          - The six trigonometric ratios in a right triangle and the naming logic
          - Exact values at 0, 30, 45, 60 and 90 degrees, rebuilt from two triangles rather than
            memorised
          - Finding all ratios from one, with Pythagoras doing the work
          - The fundamental identity and its rearrangements
          - Proving simple identities with a fixed strategy list
          - Ratio MCQs at speed: value questions in under a minute
        Projects built:
          - Two-triangle derivation page: the 30-60-90 and 45-45-90 triangles built and every standard
            value read off them
        Practice: 30 ratio evaluations and 6 identity proofs, plus one 10-question timed MCQ
        set on values
      Weeks 31-32: Heights and Distances
        Topics:
          - Angles of elevation and depression on honest, labelled figures
          - Single-triangle problems: towers, poles, kites and slopes
          - Two-triangle problems: two observation points and moving observers
          - Choosing the ratio that solves in one step
          - Rounding sensibly and sanity-checking against the figure
          - Where trigonometry goes in Class 11: a preview, not a syllabus
        Projects built:
          - Figure-first set: 8 heights and distances problems where the marked figure is drawn and
            approved before solving
        Practice: 15 heights and distances problems including 4 two-triangle setups, every
        figure labelled with the given angle
        Assessment: Month 8 test: a 25-mark trigonometry paper of ratios, identities and
        applications, one third MCQ

    Month 9: Coordinate Geometry (Weeks 33-36)
      Weeks 33-34: The Plane and Its Formulas
        Topics:
          - The Cartesian plane: plotting, quadrants and reading coordinates fluently
          - The distance formula from Pythagoras, derived and drilled
          - Classifying triangles and quadrilaterals by computed distances
          - The section formula and midpoints, with internal division problems
          - Ratios from coordinates: where the axes cut a segment
          - Sketch-first habit: every coordinate problem starts with a drawing
        Projects built:
          - Coordinate gallery: 6 figures plotted, classified and verified by distances, presented on
            graph paper
        Practice: 25 distance and section formula problems, each with a labelled sketch, plus 5
        classification questions
      Weeks 35-36: Lines and Coordinate Problem Solving
        Topics:
          - Slope as steepness: computing it and reading it from a sketch
          - Parallel and perpendicular slopes, kept concrete
          - Collinearity by slope and by distance, two roads to one answer
          - Coordinate proofs: choosing axes cleverly to make geometry easy
          - Mixed coordinate MCQs under time
          - Phase review: the toolkit chapters consolidated onto revision sheets
        Projects built:
          - Coordinate proof piece: one classical geometry fact proved by placing coordinates well,
            written up in full
        Practice: 20 slope and collinearity problems plus one timed 12-question coordinate MCQ
        set, error log updated
        Assessment: Phase 3 milestone: a 40-mark paper across mensuration, trigonometry and
        coordinates, half MCQ, fully reviewed

  ---------------------------------------------------------------
  PHASE 4: PROBLEM SOLVING AND THE MCQ PHASE (MONTHS 10-12, WEEKS 37-48)
  ---------------------------------------------------------------
  The part school never teaches: heuristics for unfamiliar problems, olympiad-style questions,
  then a full timed MCQ and mock phase in the style of NTSE-type talent exams and entrance
  papers.

    Month 10: How Hard Problems Are Actually Solved (Weeks 37-40)
      Weeks 37-38: The Heuristics
        Topics:
          - Understand, plan, execute, check: the honest version of problem solving
          - Trying small cases and looking for the pattern that survives
          - Working backwards from what is asked
          - Drawing the right diagram, and redrawing when it misleads
          - Parity and simple invariants: what cannot change no matter the moves
          - Olympiad-style number and algebra problems using the heuristics, difficulty honest but humane
        Projects built:
          - Solution journal opened: every hard problem written up with the heuristic used and the dead
            ends kept, not erased
        Practice: 8 problems for the week, chosen to need different heuristics; write-ups
        matter more than answer counts
      Weeks 39-40: Counting and Logical Structure
        Topics:
          - Systematic listing: counting without missing and without double-counting
          - The multiplication principle and simple arrangements
          - Combinations kept concrete: choosing teams and handshakes
          - The pigeonhole principle through puzzles
          - Logic puzzles: knights, liars and truth tables lite
          - Where these ideas reappear: Class 11 permutations and combinations, and reasoning sections of
            talent exams
        Projects built:
          - Counting problem set write-up: 5 counting problems solved twice, once by listing and once by
            principle, results reconciled
        Practice: 12 counting and logic problems with full write-ups in the solution journal
        Assessment: Month 10 checkpoint: a 20-mark problem-solving paper where method write-ups
        earn marks alongside answers

    Month 11: MCQ Craft Under Time (Weeks 41-44)
      Weeks 41-42: The Craft of the Multiple Choice Question
        Topics:
          - How MCQ setters build wrong options, and what that tells the solver
          - Elimination: discarding options by sign, size, units or parity
          - Option testing: substituting answers back instead of solving forwards
          - Special values: choosing convenient numbers for variable-heavy questions
          - Estimation as a weapon: bounding the answer before computing it
          - When to solve honestly: questions where shortcuts are traps
        Projects built:
          - Technique tally: 30 MCQs solved with the technique noted per question, then tallied to see
            each student's habits
        Practice: Three 15-question topic-wise MCQ sets under time, error log updated with
        technique choices, not just misses
      Weeks 43-44: Sectional Timing and the Error Log
        Topics:
          - Time budgeting: marks per minute and the discipline of moving on
          - Sectional MCQ sets across algebra, geometry, mensuration, trigonometry and coordinates
          - The two-pass strategy: bank the easy questions first
          - Guessing policy: when unanswered beats wrong, and reading the paper's rules
          - Error log analytics: which topic, which technique, which minute of the section
          - Building each student's personal weak-topic drill plan for the mock month
        Projects built:
          - Error log analysis report: the student's own two-page summary of their MCQ patterns going
            into the mocks
        Practice: Four timed sectional sets across the fortnight, each reviewed the same week,
        drill plan agreed with the teacher
        Assessment: Month 11 checkpoint: one full-length topic-mixed MCQ paper under exam
        timing, fully debriefed

    Month 12: Mocks and the Readiness Review (Weeks 45-48)
      Weeks 45-46: The Mock Series
        Topics:
          - Full-length foundation mocks in the style of NTSE-type talent exams and entrance papers
          - Exam-day routine rehearsed: instructions, bubbling, rough-work discipline
          - Review clinic after every mock: every miss classified and assigned a fix
          - Score movement read honestly: trends matter, single papers do not
          - Targeted drills between mocks from each student's plan
          - Stamina: holding accuracy in the last quarter of a long paper
        Projects built:
          - Mock file: each paper filed with its marked script, error classification and one-line fix per
            miss
        Practice: One additional mock at home under honest timing, self-marked and brought to
        the review clinic
      Weeks 47-48: Final Mocks and the Road to Class 11
        Topics:
          - Two final mocks under strict conditions, spaced for recovery
          - The readiness map: every topic rated from the year's evidence, no vibes
          - The solution journal and proof portfolio reviewed as a body of work
          - What Class 11 changes: pace, abstraction, and how this foundation meets it
          - Keeping the edge: a weekly problem habit for the months after the course
          - Course close: one-on-one review with each family
        Projects built:
          - Personal readiness map: topic-by-topic strengths and fixes, built from the error log and mock
            file
          - Completed solution journal: a year of hard problems with the student's own write-ups
        Practice: Light targeted drills only, set individually from the final error log
        Assessment: Course milestone: final full-length mock and readiness review with the
        family, plus certificate review

PROJECTS THE STUDENT BUILDS AND KEEPS

  - A proof portfolio: every major theorem of the course written in full four-part format
  - A solution journal: hard problems written up with heuristics and honest dead ends
  - A personal error log maintained from phase 1 and analysed before the mock phase
  - The identity map and circle theorem atlas, built by the student
  - A coordinate proof piece: classical geometry proved by clever axis placement
  - A scaling experiment write-up connecting length, area and volume
  - The technique tally and error log analysis report from the MCQ phase
  - A mock file with marked scripts and a final topic-by-topic readiness map

  Total projects: A year-long body of work: proof portfolio, solution journal, error log, mock file and readiness map

SKILLS THE STUDENT WILL HAVE AT THE END

  - Number theory basics: divisibility, primes, HCF-LCM and remainder thinking
  - Algebra at depth: exponents, surds, identities, factorisation, equations and inequalities
  - Proof writing across congruence, similarity, quadrilaterals and circle theorems
  - Mensuration, introductory trigonometry and coordinate geometry to entrance-exam standard
  - Problem-solving heuristics: small cases, working backwards, invariants and clean diagrams
  - Timed MCQ craft: elimination, option testing, time budgeting and error-log-driven improvement

HOW A TYPICAL WEEK IS SPLIT

  Live classes: 2 live one-hour classes per week; mock sittings in month 12 run longer for full
    papers
  Practice: 3-4 hours weekly of problem sets, proofs and journal write-ups between classes
  Review: Problem sets marked with written feedback; proofs and journal entries reviewed line
    by line each month
  Homework: A problem set after every class, and a monthly mixed-review assignment that
    deliberately folds in earlier topics

SUPPORT INCLUDED

  Doubt support: WhatsApp doubt support between classes, with worked solutions for stuck
    problems
  Progress updates: Monthly progress notes to parents with test scores, error-log trends and
    the current readiness picture

CERTIFICATION DETAIL

  Completion: Certificate from Modern Age Coders, awarded on passing the final assessment. Fall

    attendance

WHERE THIS CAN LEAD

  - Class 11 maths in the science stream, entered with algebra and geometry that do not need
    repair
  - Formal JEE preparation from Class 11, with the foundation layer already done
  - Olympiad tracks such as IOQM for students who discover they enjoy the hard problems
  - School exams along the way: the depth here makes board-level questions feel routine
  - Our data science and programming courses, where the same structured thinking transfers
    directly

COMMON QUESTIONS ABOUT THIS COURSE

  For anything about cost, use PART 4 and RULE 1. Do not quote two regions.

  Q: What exactly is a foundation course? Is this JEE coaching for a 13-year-old?
  A: No, and be wary of anything that says otherwise. JEE tests Class 11 and 12 material; no
  Class 8 student should be solving JEE papers. A foundation course strengthens the Class 8 to
  10 layer that JEE preparation later stands on: algebra done at depth, geometry actually
  proved, and the problem-solving and MCQ habits school never teaches. Students who arrive in
  Class 11 with that layer solid cope with the pace; students who arrive with gaps spend Class
  11 repairing them.

  Q: Do you promise selection in JEE or any exam?
  A: No. Nobody can honestly promise a selection or a rank, least of all three or four years
  out, and we think enrolling a 13-year-old on the back of such a promise is wrong. What we
  commit to is specific: the full curriculum taught at depth, marked work with written
  feedback, a proof portfolio and solution journal the student builds, a timed mock series, and
  honest monthly reporting on exactly where the student stands.

  Q: Is this course NTSE preparation? Is NTSE even happening?
  A: We are careful here because many courses are not: NCERT suspended the National Talent
  Search Scheme, and the exam has not been conducted since the 2021-22 cycle, with the scheme
  stalled until further orders. There has been talk of a revamped revival, but nothing a family
  should plan around. We use NTSE-style papers in the mock phase because the format is
  excellent training, and if the exam returns our students will be ready for it, but nobody
  should enrol anywhere on the promise of an exam that is currently not running.

  Q: Which class is the right time to start, 8, 9 or 10?
  A: Any of the three works, which is why batches are separated by class. Starting in Class 8
  gives the most room: depth can build gradually with no exam pressure. Class 9 is the most
  common entry point and aligns well, since Class 9 NCERT is where proofs and harder algebra
  begin. Class 10 students run the same arc with board preparation happening in parallel, and
  the overlap actually helps, because the foundation depth makes board questions feel easy.

  Q: Will this clash with what school teaches?
  A: No, because the course is NCERT-aligned by design. We teach the same chapters school does,
  in a compatible order, and go deeper rather than sideways: harder problem forms, the proofs
  behind the formulas, and extensions school skips for time. Most families find school marks
  improve as a side effect, since school papers sample the easier end of what students here
  practise weekly.

  Q: What are the olympiad-style problems? Is this an olympiad course?
  A: It is not a dedicated olympiad course; serious olympiad preparation for exams like IOQM is
  its own track with its own syllabus. What we teach in month 10 is the thinking style
  olympiads reward: heuristics like small cases, working backwards and invariants, practised on
  genuinely unfamiliar problems at a humane difficulty. Students who light up during that phase
  get pointed, honestly, toward proper olympiad training as a next step.

  Q: How much homework should we expect?
  A: Three to four hours a week: problem sets after each class, proof write-ups during the
  geometry phase, journal entries during the problem-solving phase, and timed papers in the
  final months. The write-ups are non-negotiable, because this course grades reasoning, not
  answer lists. It is a real commitment, and we would rather say so now than surprise you in
  month 2.

  Q: How am I assessed, and is the certificate just for showing up?
  A: No. A problem set follows every class with written feedback, monthly reviews deliberately
  mix new material with earlier topics so nothing is forgotten, and the course ends with a full
  mock paper as the final assessment. Passing earns the certificate; falling short earns
  focused revision and a free retest. We measure real understanding, not attendance.

  Q: Can we try a class before enrolling?
  A: Yes, the first demo class is free and carries no obligation. Book it at
  learn.modernagecoders.com/contact or message us on WhatsApp at +91 91233 66161. The demo
  includes a short diagnostic, after which the teacher will tell you plainly whether the
  student is ready for this course or better served by our school maths courses first.

  To enrol, message Shivam Sir on +91 9123366161 or send the parent this link: https://learn.modernagecoders.com/courses/jee-foundation-maths-course-class-8-10
  For a demo: the Priority Live Demo (guaranteed, today or tomorrow) is booked at
  https://learn.modernagecoders.com/priority-demo . The free demo is a waiting list with no fixed date.

  more months in hand for learners who need them. The three teaching phases build the language
  and its real-world domain; the finale month ships a capstone and sits the final exam.

  ends with a final exam: a practical build plus written questions from the whole syllabus.
  Passing earns the certificate; falling short earns focused revision and a free retest.

  interop is explained where it matters (older codebases), but modern Android development, and

  your account; what the course guarantees is an app and a release checklist that are genuinely
  ready for it.

Subject area: Data Science Mathematics
Designed for: Working professionals

Time needed: 2 live classes/week + 4-6 hours practice

PRICE FOR THIS COURSE (quote only the one that applies to the person asking)
  In India, per month:      group Rs 1,499, mini batch Rs 2,999, one to one Rs 4,999
  Outside India, per month: group $100, one to one $150
  Classes: group and mini batch two live classes a week, eight a month; one to one in India one

WHAT THIS COURSE IS

  Maths for data science, live online: statistics, probability, linear algebra, regression, ML
  mathematics, Bayesian methods and A/B testing in 12-14 months.

  In one line: The difference between running models and understanding them is mathematics. This is that mathematics, taught honestly in twelve months.

ABOUT THE PROGRAMME

  Every data career eventually hits the same wall: the tools are easy, the mathematics behind
  them is not, and interviews, promotions and real analytical judgment all live on the far side
  of that wall. This live online course teaches exactly the mathematics data work stands on:
  statistics that tell the truth, probability that calibrates uncertainty, the linear algebra
  inside every model, regression and classification understood from first principles,
  optimization, the mathematics of neural networks, Bayesian methods, time series, and the
  experimental design behind honest A/B testing. The course is deliberately practical about
  rigor: every concept is derived enough to be owned, then immediately exercised on real data
  questions, the kind analysts and data scientists actually face. Statistical malpractice gets
  named and corrected throughout: p-hacking, leakage, confounding, the graph that lies. By the
  end, a student does not just know the formulas; they know which analysis is honest and can
  defend it in an interview or a meeting. The pace is real: two live classes a week plus four
  to six hours of practice fits the syllabus in twelve months, and learners who need longer
  take up to fourteen, the batch adapts. Assessment is honest too: problem sets after every
  class, monthly mixed reviews that reach back deliberately, phase exams, and a final exam that
  decides the certificate, with focused revision and a free retest for those who fall short.
  Real knowledge, real work, depth over dopamine.

WHAT MAKES THIS COURSE DIFFERENT

  - Mathematics first, tools second: understanding that transfers across every library and
    language
  - Interview-honest coverage: the statistics, linear algebra and ML mathematics that data
    interviews actually probe
  - Statistical malpractice named and corrected: p-hacking, leakage, confounding and misleading
    charts, studied on purpose
  - Every concept lands on real data: derivations earn their keep in applied exercises the same
    week
  - An honest 12-month arc with 2 months of margin: learners who need more time take up to 14,
    nobody is rushed
  - Real assessment: weekly problem sets, monthly mixed reviews, and a final exam that decides
    the certificate, with focused revision and a free retest

THE LEARNING PATH, STEP BY STEP

  Phase 1: Statistics that tell the truth (Months 1-3): descriptive statistics, visualization,
  probability and the great distributions
  Phase 2: Linear algebra and inference (Months 4-6): vectors to PCA, sampling, confidence
  intervals and hypothesis testing done honestly
  Phase 3: The mathematics of machine learning (Months 7-9): regression from first principles,
  classification, trees, clustering and evaluation
  Phase 4: Modern practice (Months 10-12): optimization, neural network mathematics, Bayesian
  methods, time series, A/B testing and the capstone

WHAT A STUDENT NEEDS BEFORE STARTING

  Maths background: School mathematics (Class 12 or equivalent). Calculus is refreshed where
    needed; no university maths assumed
  Coding background: Helpful but not required; the mathematics is the syllabus, with
    spreadsheets and light Python used as calculators
  Equipment: A computer with a stable internet connection
  Age: College students and working professionals (18+)
  Time commitment: 2 live classes plus 4-6 hours of practice a week

WHO THIS COURSE IS FOR

  Aspiring analysts: Students and professionals aiming at data analyst and data science roles
    who keep hitting the maths wall
  Tool users: People fluent in Excel, SQL or pandas who want to finally understand what the
    numbers are doing
  Interview candidates: Candidates whose next round is statistics, probability and ML
    fundamentals
  Ml learners: Students in ML courses who realize the mathematics was assumed, not taught
  Decision makers: Managers and founders who want to read analyses and experiments without
    being fooled

COMMON QUESTIONS ABOUT THIS COURSE

  For anything about cost, use PART 4 and RULE 1. Do not quote two regions.

  Q: What exactly does this maths for data science course teach?
  A: The mathematics data careers actually stand on, in four phases: statistics and probability
  that tell the truth; linear algebra through eigenvalues and PCA plus honest statistical
  inference; the mathematics of machine learning, regression, classification, trees, clustering
  and evaluation from first principles; and modern practice, optimization, neural network
  mathematics, Bayesian methods, time series and A/B testing, ending in a capstone analysis on
  real data.

  Q: How long does it take to learn the maths for data science?
  A: Honestly: 12 months at 2 live classes a week plus 4 to 6 hours of practice, and the course
  keeps 2 months of margin in hand for learners who need more repetition, up to 14 months with
  no penalty. Crash courses compress this into weeks by skipping the understanding; the wall
  they skip is exactly what interviews and real work then test.

  Q: How is progress measured? Is the certificate just for attending?
  A: No. Problem sets follow every class and come back with written feedback, monthly reviews
  deliberately mix new material with earlier topics so nothing fades, each phase ends with an
  exam, and the course ends with a final exam, written plus practical, that decides the
  certificate. Falling short earns a focused revision plan and a free retest. The certificate
  certifies knowledge, not attendance.

  Q: Do I need to know programming or calculus already?
  A: Neither. School mathematics is the entry bar; the calculus that appears is refreshed as
  needed, and code is used only as a calculator, spreadsheets and light Python, because the
  mathematics is the syllabus. Students who already code simply see the connections faster.

  Q: How is this different from a data science bootcamp?
  A: Bootcamps teach tools and hope the mathematics arrives by osmosis; it does not. This
  course is the missing layer: the statistics, linear algebra and ML mathematics that make tool
  skills defensible in interviews and reliable at work. The two pair well, our Data Analysis
  course covers the tooling side, and this course makes it mean something.

  Q: Will this help me in analytics interviews and real work?
  A: Directly: probability puzzles, hypothesis testing, regression interpretation, evaluation
  metrics and A/B test design are the exact backbone of analytics and data science interviews,
  and the course drills them with written defense, not just computation. At work, the payoff is
  judgment: knowing which analysis is honest, and being the person in the room who can say why.

  Q: Does this cover deep learning and AI?
  A: It covers their mathematics honestly: optimization, gradient descent and the mathematics
  of neural networks, computed by hand on small networks, plus a clear map of where
  transformers and attention sit. Full deep learning practice, building and training real
  models, is our AI and Machine Learning Masterclass, which assumes exactly the mathematics
  this course builds.

  Q: Can I take a trial class?
  A: Yes, a free demo class with no commitment: book at learn.modernagecoders.com/contact or
  message us on WhatsApp at +91 91233 66161. Bring a statistics question from your own work or
  study; the demo is best when it runs on your real problem. (Agent note: the free demo is a
  waiting list with no fixed date. The Priority Live Demo is a guaranteed class today or
  tomorrow, booked at https://learn.modernagecoders.com/priority-demo . Offer both, as RULE 3
  says.)

  Q: Are lessons live or self-paced videos?
  A: Live, always: small groups where problems are worked together and your reasoning gets
  corrected in real time, never pre-recorded videos. Mathematical judgment is built under
  feedback; a video cannot tell you why your hypothesis test is invalid.

COMMON QUESTIONS ABOUT THIS COURSE

  For anything about cost, use PART 4 and RULE 1. Do not quote two regions.

  Q: What does the olympiad mathematics program cover?
  A: The 12 month curriculum works through the four classical olympiad pillars: number theory
  and combinatorics, competition algebra with polynomials and functional equations, Euclidean
  and coordinate geometry with trigonometry, and inequalities with advanced problem solving
  strategy, ending in mock competitions. The goal is genuine problem solving depth, not
  memorized tricks.

  Q: Which competitions does this prepare students for?
  A: The training maps to the Indian olympiad pipeline, IOQM leading toward RMO and INMO, plus
  NMTC and SOF style olympiads, and the same material serves AMC and AIME aspirants since the
  topic areas overlap heavily. We prepare students honestly for the level they are at, and we
  never promise medals or ranks, because no honest program can.

  Q: Is my child ready for this course?
  A: It suits students with a strong grasp of school mathematics who enjoy hard problems,
  typically from middle school upward. It is not designed for closing school level gaps;
  students who need foundations first are better served by our school mathematics programs and
  can graduate into this one.

  Q: What are the prerequisites?
  A: Solid school algebra and geometry, care in reading mathematical statements, and a genuine
  appetite for problems that take longer than five minutes. Competition maths rewards
  consistent weekly practice more than raw talent, so expect a serious commitment.

  Q: How is progress measured in competition maths?
  A: Through weekly problem sets at calibrated difficulty, a personal problem log tracking
  which techniques are secure, and regular timed mock papers in the final months. Progress here
  looks like solving harder problems more independently, and the log makes that visible.

  Q: How is my child assessed, and is the certificate just for attending?
  A: No. A problem set follows every class with written feedback, monthly reviews deliberately
  mix new material with earlier topics so nothing is forgotten, each phase ends with a
  cumulative exam, and the course ends with a final exam covering the whole syllabus. Passing
  earns the certificate; falling short earns focused revision and a free retest. We measure
  understanding, not attendance.

  Q: Can we try a session first?
  A: Yes, book a free demo class at learn.modernagecoders.com/contact with no commitment; we
  use it to gauge your child's current problem solving level and to recommend honestly whether
  this course or a foundations course fits better. WhatsApp +91 91233 66161 for quick
  questions. (Agent note: the free demo is a waiting list with no fixed date. The Priority Live
  Demo is a guaranteed class today or tomorrow, booked at
  https://learn.modernagecoders.com/priority-demo . Offer both, as RULE 3 says.)

  Q: What is the class format?
  A: Live one hour online classes with a real teacher in deliberately small groups, never
  recorded lectures. Students present their attempts and the mentor works the reasoning with
  them, which is the only way competition thinking actually develops.

  Q: Is there a certificate, and what else does my child take away?
  A: Yes, an Olympiad Mathematics Excellence Certificate on completion, plus the more valuable
  artifact: a documented problem portfolio and mock paper record showing the level reached.
  That evidence outlasts any single contest result.

WHAT THIS COURSE IS

  Live course where kids ages 10-15 learn maths by coding it: fractions, algebra, geometry and
  probability built as Python projects. Small live batches or 1-on-1, free demo.

  In one line: If you can build it, you understand it. Students build the maths.

ABOUT THE PROGRAMME

  A 9-month live course teaching mathematics the way our whole school believes it should be
  met: by building it. Students write Python programs that ARE the maths, a fraction simplifier
  that forces understanding of GCD, turtle geometry that makes angles visceral, probability
  simulators that settle arguments with ten thousand dice rolls, and function grapher projects
  that turn algebra into something you can watch. This is the signature Modern Age Coders
  fusion, taught by mentors genuinely fluent in both subjects, and for Ontario families, it
  happens to cover the coding expectations now examined inside math class from Grade 1. No
  prior coding needed; the mathematics runs roughly grades 5-9 territory with stretch room.

WHAT MAKES THIS COURSE DIFFERENT

  - The maths is the syllabus, the code is the method: every program exists to force a
    mathematical idea into the open
  - A computer rejects vague understanding, code that half-understands fractions simply does not
    run, which makes debugging a mathematics lesson
  - Mentors fluent in both subjects, because a coding teacher who waves at the maths (or vice
    versa) breaks the whole idea
  - Real Python from week one, at a pace built for ages 10-15
  - Every topic ends with a working artifact the student built and can demo
  - Directly serves Ontario's coding-in-math strand, and the computational-thinking push in
    curricula worldwide
  - The engagement answer for the child who says maths is boring but plays with code for hours,
    or the reverse
  - One dedicated mentor, one full interactive hour, twice a week

THE LEARNING PATH, STEP BY STEP

  Phase 1: Numbers as programs: Python foundations through arithmetic, divisibility, fractions
  and number patterns
  Phase 2: Shape and change: turtle geometry, coordinates, and algebra brought alive through
  variables, functions and graphing
  Phase 3: Chance and data: probability simulators, statistics on real datasets, and a capstone
  project of the student's own design

WHAT A STUDENT NEEDS BEFORE STARTING

  Education: Ages 10-15 (roughly grades 5-10)
  Math background: Comfortable whole-number arithmetic; everything else is built inside the
    course
  Coding experience: None required, Python taught from zero
  Equipment: Computer with stable internet; free tools only (no purchases)
  English: Course taught in English
  Motivation: Curiosity about either half, maths or code, is enough; the course supplies the
    other

WHO THIS COURSE IS FOR

  Bored by worksheets: The child who says maths is boring but builds in Minecraft for hours
  Maths lovers: The child who loves maths and deserves the best maths toy ever made

  Understanding seekers: Students who pass tests but want (or need) the ideas to actually make

FULL CURRICULUM, WEEK BY WEEK

  This is the complete teaching plan. Parents can ask about any week.

  ---------------------------------------------------------------
  PHASE 1: NUMBERS AS PROGRAMS (MONTHS 1-3)
  ---------------------------------------------------------------
  Python foundations learned through number theory a student can touch: parity, divisibility,

    Month 1: First Programs, First Number Ideas (Weeks 1-4)

        you see.

        detectors and cycle patterns
      Conditionals and Divisibility Rules
        Topics:
          - if, elif and else

          - Explaining divisibility rules backwards
          - Combining conditions

        Projects built:

        Practice: Code a divisibility checker for 2, 3 and 5 and explain in your own words why

COMMON QUESTIONS ABOUT THIS COURSE

  For anything about cost, use PART 4 and RULE 1. Do not quote two regions.

  Q: Is this a maths course or a coding course?
  A: A maths course that uses code as its laboratory. The syllabus is mathematical, number
  theory, fractions, geometry, algebra, probability, statistics, and every program exists to
  force one of those ideas into the open. Students do finish with real Python skills, which is
  a genuine bonus, but the mathematics is the star.

  Q: Does my child need coding experience?
  A: None. Python is taught from the first hello, at a pace built for ages 10-15. Children who
  already code a little move faster into the mathematical meat; the mentor adjusts either way.

  Q: Why does building things teach maths better than practicing problems?
  A: Because a computer rejects vague understanding. A student who 'sort of' knows fraction
  equivalence writes a simplifier that fails, and fixing it requires actually understanding
  GCD. That debugging loop, predict, test, explain the gap, is the deepest mathematical
  practice there is, and it feels like play.

  Q: We're in Ontario and coding is now examined inside math class. Does this help?
  A: Directly, this course is our sweet spot for exactly that curriculum. Ontario weaves coding
  expectations through math from Grade 1, most homes have nobody fluent in both halves, and our
  mentors teach both natively. Students walk back into class ahead on the strand instead of
  puzzled by it.

  Q: My child loves games but says maths is boring. Will this work?
  A: This course exists for that child. The maths arrives wearing a project the child wants to
  build, angle art, a dice game, a grapher, and engagement does the heavy lifting. The reverse
  child (loves maths, indifferent to screens) discovers code as the best maths toy ever made.

  Q: What maths level does it assume and reach?
  A: It starts from comfortable whole-number arithmetic (roughly grade 5) and reaches into
  linear functions, probability and statistics (roughly grade 9 territory), with stretch room
  for strong students. It runs happily alongside any school curriculum and strengthens it
  rather than clashing.

  Q: How am I assessed, and is the certificate just for showing up?
  A: No. A problem set follows every class with written feedback, monthly reviews deliberately
  mix new material with earlier topics so nothing is forgotten, and the course ends with a
  final exam plus a portfolio of working maths programs. Passing earns the certificate; falling
  short earns focused revision and a free retest. We measure real understanding, not
  attendance.

  Q: Can we try it before paying?
  A: Yes. Every student starts with a free live demo class, they will build and run their first
  small program inside that hour, and you will see the method working with your own child. No
  card details required.

ABOUT THE PROGRAMME

  A 12-month live program that builds genuine mental arithmetic in children aged 5-10, the
  honest alternative to abacus franchises and 'Vedic tricks' courses. Trick-based speed
  impresses at demos and quietly expires: it bypasses understanding, so it cannot transfer to
  fractions, algebra or problem solving. We build number sense instead, numbers as decomposable
  quantities, number bonds, compensation and estimation, through games and puzzles a child
  genuinely enjoys. The result is a child who calculates fast because they see numbers clearly,
  and that clarity keeps paying through every year of school mathematics.

WHAT MAKES THIS COURSE DIFFERENT

FULL CURRICULUM, WEEK BY WEEK

  This is the complete teaching plan. Parents can ask about any week.

  ---------------------------------------------------------------
  PHASE 1: NUMBER SENSE FOUNDATIONS (MONTHS 1-4)
  ---------------------------------------------------------------
  Before speed comes seeing: numbers as quantities that break apart and recombine. This phase
  builds subitizing, part-whole thinking and the bonds of 10 and 20 through concrete materials
  and games, tuned to each child's starting stage.

    Month 1: Seeing Numbers (Weeks 1-4)
      Getting to Know Your Number Sense
        Topics:
          - Counting games that show how far a child counts with ease
          - Quick quantity flashes to see which small numbers are known on sight
          - Simple addition play that reveals the current strategy (counting on, known facts, or
            guessing)
          - Noticing confidence and comfort with numbers, not only right answers
          - Spotting facts already automatic, such as small doubles or bonds
          - Setting a friendly starting point tuned to the child, not the age
        Practice: Over a snack, ask your child to grab a small handful of raisins and guess how
        many before counting, then count together to check, keeping it light and playful.
        Detail: Playful diagnostic: which facts, strategies and confidence the child already
        holds, disguised as games
      Seeing How Many at a Glance
        Topics:
          - Recognising 1 to 5 dots instantly without counting (subitizing)
          - Reading dice patterns as whole amounts
          - Meeting the ten-frame as a picture of numbers
          - Seeing 6 to 10 as a small group sitting on top of five
          - Flashing and hiding quantities to build quick recognition
          - Talking about how the amount was seen, not just the answer
        Practice: Roll one die a few times each evening and race to say the number before
        counting the dots, and whoever spots it first wins that round.
        Detail: Subitizing and quantity sense: dots, dice and ten-frames, recognising amounts
        without counting
      Numbers Are Made of Smaller Numbers
        Topics:
          - Breaking a small number into two parts in different ways
          - Seeing 7 as 5 and 2, 6 and 1, or 4 and 3
          - Using fingers or counters to split a group across two hands
          - Understanding that the parts always rebuild the whole
          - Finding every way to make a chosen number
          - Explaining a split out loud in the child's own words
        Practice: Give your child 6 buttons and ask how many ways they can split them into two
        piles, writing each way down together like a treasure list.
        Detail: Part-whole thinking: every number is made of other numbers (7 is 5-and-2,
        6-and-1, 3-and-4)
      Living on the Number Line
        Topics:
          - Placing numbers in order along a line
          - Deciding which number is bigger from its position
          - Measuring the distance or jump between two numbers
          - Hopping forwards and backwards along the line
          - Meeting the empty number line as a thinking tool
          - Estimating where a number belongs before checking
        Practice: Draw a long line on paper with 0 at one end and 10 at the other, then take
        turns pointing to where numbers like 7 or 3 should sit.
        Detail: The number line as home: position, order, distance and the empty-number-line
        game

    Months 2-3: The Bonds That Power Everything (Weeks 5-12)
      The Pairs That Make Ten
        Topics:
          - Finding both parts that add to make 10
          - Recognising 6 and 4, 7 and 3, 8 and 2 as ten-friends
          - Using ten-frames to see the missing part
          - Answering ten-bonds quickly through repeated play
          - Spotting a ten-bond hidden inside a larger problem
          - Building speed through fun, never flashcard pressure
        Practice: Play make ten: you say a number under ten and your child shouts the partner
        that finishes the ten, then swap roles after five turns.
        Detail: Bonds of 10 to automaticity, through games, never flashcard grind
      Doubles and Their Neighbours
        Topics:
          - Learning the doubles up to 10 plus 10 as anchor facts
          - Using a known double to solve a near-double (6 plus 7 is double 6 and one more)
          - Adding 9 by adding 10 and stepping back one
          - Adding 11 by adding 10 and stepping up one
          - Seeing how one known fact unlocks several nearby ones
          - Choosing the closest double to lean on
        Practice: At bedtime, call out a double like double 4 for a quick answer, then a
        near-double like 4 plus 5, and let your child explain how the double helped.
        Detail: Doubles and near-doubles as anchor facts; adding 9 and 11 by compensation
        preview
      Making Ten to Add Bigger
        Topics:
          - Splitting the second number to fill up to ten first
          - Turning 8 plus 5 into 10 plus 3
          - Using ten-frames to see the bridge across ten
          - Knowing how much a number needs to reach ten
          - Adding the leftover part after reaching ten
          - Choosing make-ten when numbers sit close to ten
        Practice: With two ten-frames and some counters, set up sums like 8 plus 5 and let your
        child slide counters to fill the first ten, then read the answer.
        Detail: Bridging through 10: the make-ten strategy that turns 8+5 into 10+3
      Bonds to Twenty and Fact Families
        Topics:
          - Finding pairs that add to make 20
          - Linking a ten-bond to its twenty partner
          - Seeing a fact family: 13 plus 7, 7 plus 13, 20 minus 7, 20 minus 13
          - Understanding addition and subtraction as two views of one picture
          - Using a known adding fact to find its subtracting partner
          - Building all four facts from one number trio
        Practice: Pick three numbers that fit together, like 6, 4 and 10, and challenge your
        child to say all four facts they can make from them.
        Detail: Bonds to 20 and fact families: addition and subtraction as one idea seen from
        two sides

    Month 4: Subtraction as Distance + Stage Checkpoint (Weeks 13-16)
      Two Ways to Subtract
        Topics:
          - Taking away by counting back from the larger number
          - Finding the gap by counting up between the numbers
          - Deciding which way is faster for a given problem
          - Seeing subtraction as the distance between two numbers
          - Using the number line to picture both methods
          - Explaining which route was chosen and why
        Practice: Ask a shopping question like you have 10 and a toy costs 8, how much change,
        and let your child try both counting back and counting up to compare.
        Detail: Subtraction two ways: taking away versus finding the gap, and when each is
        faster
      The Shopkeeper's Counting-Up Trick
        Topics:
          - Counting up from the price to the money paid
          - Using friendly stops like the next ten
          - Adding the small jumps to find the change
          - Seeing why counting up avoids hard take-away sums
          - Playing shop with real or pretend coins
          - Checking the change makes sense
        Practice: Set up a tiny pretend shop with priced items and let your child be the
        shopkeeper, counting up from the price to give you the right change.
        Detail: Counting up for change: the shopkeeper's method every adult secretly uses
      Many Roads to the Same Answer
        Topics:
          - Solving one problem in more than one way
          - Sharing a strategy out loud in a number talk
          - Listening to a different route to the same total
          - Comparing which method felt quickest
          - Respecting that different minds pick different paths
          - Naming the strategy used (make-ten, doubles, or counting up)
        Practice: Give one sum like 7 plus 8 and ask your child for two different ways to solve
        it, then you share a third way you thought of.
        Detail: Mixed strategy play: number talks where children compare routes to the same
        answer
      Phase One Check Through Play
        Topics:
          - Revisiting bonds of 10 and 20 through games
          - Choosing a strategy for each problem confidently
          - Explaining the thinking behind an answer
          - Teaching a strategy back to the mentor or a parent
          - Celebrating the facts now known by heart
          - Noticing which few facts still want more play
        Practice: Let your child be the teacher for ten minutes and show you one number
        strategy they learned this phase, explaining each step.
        Assessment: A relaxed review game covering number bonds, part-whole thinking and the
        early strategies, where the child solves a problem, explains it, and teaches a
        favourite method back, with no timing or pressure.
        Detail: Stage mastery check through games: solve it, explain it, teach it back

  ---------------------------------------------------------------
  PHASE 2: THE STRATEGY TOOLKIT (MONTHS 5-8)
  ---------------------------------------------------------------
  The heart of mental maths: named strategies the child chooses between, make-ten,
  compensation, doubling and halving, plus multiplication met as structure and arrays rather
  than chanted tables. Choice is the skill; speed is the side effect.

    Month 5: Two-Digit Courage (Weeks 17-20)
      Adding Two-Digit Numbers in Jumps
        Topics:
          - Adding the tens first in one jump
          - Then adding the leftover ones
          - Using an empty number line to record the jumps
          - Holding the running total in mind
          - Solving sums like 34 plus 23 step by step
          - Checking the answer feels about right
        Practice: Call out a two-digit sum like 42 plus 30 during a car ride and ask your child
        to jump the tens out loud, then add any ones.
        Detail: Adding two-digit numbers mentally: jumps of ten, then the leftover ones
      The Compensation Superpower
        Topics:
          - Rounding a number up to a friendly ten
          - Adjusting the other number to keep the total fair
          - Turning 39 plus 26 into 40 plus 25
          - Subtracting 19 by taking 20 and giving one back
          - Understanding why the give-and-take keeps it equal
          - Choosing compensation when a number sits near a ten
        Practice: Give a near-ten sum like 29 plus 14 and let your child bump the 29 up to 30,
        solve it, then give the one back at the end.
        Detail: Compensation as a superpower: 39 + 26 becomes 40 + 25; subtracting 19 by taking
        20 and giving one back

    Month 6: Multiplication as Structure (Weeks 21-24)
      Multiplication as Groups You Can See
        Topics:
          - Making equal groups with objects
          - Building rows and columns as an array
          - Reading 3 rows of 4 as three fours
          - Connecting repeated addition to multiplication
          - Seeing that an array can be counted two ways
          - Using the words times and groups of
        Practice: Arrange snacks or blocks into equal rows, like 3 rows of 5, and ask your
        child to find the total by seeing the groups rather than counting one by one.
        Detail: Multiplication as groups and arrays, seen and built before recited
      The Clever Route Through the Tables
        Topics:
          - Learning the easy 2s, 5s and 10s first
          - Doubling the 2s to reach the 4s
          - Doubling the 4s to reach the 8s
          - Finding 9s by using 10s and stepping back a group
          - Seeing how known tables build the harder ones
          - Using skip counting as a rhythm for each table
        Practice: Practise one table a day by skip counting it like a chant on the walk to the
        door, starting with the easy 2s, 5s or 10s.
        Detail: The clever tables route: 2s, 10s and 5s first, then doubling to 4s and 8s; 9s
        by compensation

    Month 7: The Full Tables, Owned (Weeks 25-28)
      Taming the Trickiest Facts
        Topics:
          - Learning the 3s by skip counting and grouping
          - Reaching the 6s by doubling the 3s
          - Meeting the square facts like 6 times 6 and 7 times 7
          - Spotting the small handful of facts that feel hardest
          - Using a known nearby fact to reach a tricky one
          - Practising just the stubborn facts, not the whole grid
        Practice: Pick the one fact your child finds hardest this week and turn it into a silly
        rhyme or picture together to make it stick.
        Detail: 3s, 6s and the tricky squares; the handful of hard facts isolated and conquered
      Division Is Multiplication Backwards
        Topics:
          - Seeing division as sharing into equal groups
          - Linking 3 times 4 is 12 to 12 shared by 4 is 3
          - Building the multiplication and division fact family
          - Using a known times fact to answer a divide fact
          - Playing fact-family games for speed
          - Understanding remainders as leftovers, gently
        Practice: Share a small pile of objects equally between two or three plates and ask
        your child which times fact just proved the answer.
        Detail: Division as the other side of multiplication; fact-family fluency through games

    Month 8: Doubling, Halving and Strategy Choice (Weeks 29-32)
      Doubling and Halving Magic
        Topics:
          - Halving one number while doubling the other
          - Turning 16 times 5 into 8 times 10
          - Seeing why the answer stays the same
          - Choosing which number to halve to make it easy
          - Using this to multiply by 5 quickly
          - Chaining a halve and a double smoothly
        Practice: Offer a times-five problem like 14 times 5 and let your child halve the 14 to
        7 and double the 5 to 10, then read off 7 times 10.
        Detail: Doubling and halving chains: 16 x 5 as 8 x 10, the strategy that feels like
        magic and is pure structure
      Strategy Tournament and Phase Two Check
        Topics:
          - Solving one problem several different ways
          - Deciding which strategy suits which problem
          - Explaining why a chosen route was quickest
          - Reviewing make-ten, compensation and doubling-halving
          - Owning the full multiplication and division facts
          - Thinking about one's own thinking
        Practice: Hold a friendly strategy tournament: give one problem and see how many
        different correct routes your child can find and name.
        Assessment: A relaxed review game across the strategy toolkit, where the child picks
        and explains a strategy for each problem and teaches a favourite one back, with no
        timing pressure.
        Detail: Strategy tournaments: same problem, different routes, and the metacognition of
        choosing, plus stage mastery check

  ---------------------------------------------------------------
  PHASE 3: BIG NUMBERS, ESTIMATION AND DURABLE SPEED (MONTHS 9-12)
  ---------------------------------------------------------------
  The toolkit scales up: multi-digit mental arithmetic, the beginnings of fraction sense,
  estimation as judgment, and, now that understanding holds, genuine speed work. The course
  closes with each child measurably faster and, more importantly, able to explain every move.

    Month 9: Multi-Digit Mental Arithmetic (Weeks 33-36)
      Big Numbers Without Fear
        Topics:
          - Jumping by hundreds and tens using place value
          - Adding to a friendly round number first
          - Using compensation on larger numbers
          - Adding numbers like 240 plus 130 in the head
          - Keeping the place values lined up while jumping
          - Checking the size of the answer makes sense
        Practice: During a walk, add house or page numbers like 120 plus 60, encouraging your
        child to jump the hundreds and tens out loud.
        Detail: Hundreds without fear: place-value jumps, friendly numbers and compensation at
        scale
      Multiplying Beyond the Tables
        Topics:
          - Splitting a two-digit number into tens and ones
          - Multiplying each part then adding (23 times 4 is 20 times 4 plus 3 times 4)
          - Using halving and doubling on bigger products
          - Choosing the neatest way to split a number
          - Holding partial answers in mind to combine
          - Estimating first to check the result
        Practice: Give a problem like 21 times 3 and let your child split it into 20 times 3
        and 1 times 3, then add the two parts.
        Detail: Mental multiplication beyond tables: 23 x 4 by splitting, 15 x 6 by
        halving-doubling

    Month 10: Estimation as Judgment (Weeks 37-40)
      Rounding to Get Close Fast
        Topics:
          - Rounding a number to the nearest ten or hundred
          - Using rounded numbers for a quick estimate
          - Deciding how close an estimate needs to be
          - Comparing an estimate to the real answer
          - Rounding both numbers before adding
          - Understanding when an estimate is enough
        Practice: At the shop, ask your child to round a couple of prices and guess the rough
        total before you reach the till, then compare with the real total.
        Detail: Rounding with purpose: getting close fast, and knowing how close is close
        enough
      Does This Answer Make Sense?
        Topics:
          - Checking whether an answer looks reasonable
          - Using an estimate to catch a big mistake
          - Spotting answers that are far too big or too small
          - Asking about how much this should be first
          - Trusting number sense over a typed answer
          - Explaining why an answer cannot be right
        Practice: Say a deliberately silly answer to an easy sum, like 3 plus 4 is 30, and let
        your child catch it and explain why it is wrong.
        Detail: The reasonableness habit: catching wrong answers by sense, the skill
        calculators cannot replace

    Month 11: Fraction Sense Beginnings (Weeks 41-44)
      Halves and Quarters of Things
        Topics:
          - Splitting a shape or group into equal parts
          - Finding half of a quantity, like half of 12
          - Finding a quarter by halving twice
          - Seeing halves and quarters in real objects
          - Understanding fair, equal shares
          - Reading a simple fraction from a picture
        Practice: Share a snack fairly and ask your child for half, then a quarter, of a small
        group of items, checking the shares are equal.
        Detail: Halves, quarters and the fraction-of-a-quantity game, mental fractions from
        pictures
      Half, Point Five and Fifty Percent
        Topics:
          - Seeing one-half written as 0.5
          - Meeting fifty percent as another name for half
          - Linking a quarter to 0.25 and 25 percent
          - Understanding these are the same amount in different clothes
          - Spotting halves and percents in everyday life
          - Reading these friendly numbers with confidence
        Practice: Point out a half price or 50 percent off sign and ask your child what that
        means for a simple price, like half of 10.
        Detail: Fraction and decimal friends: one-half is 0.5 is 50%, the bridge built early

    Month 12: Speed With Understanding + Graduation (Weeks 45-52)
      Beat Your Own Record
        Topics:
          - Using known strategies quickly and calmly
          - Timing oneself gently to beat a personal best
          - Tracking progress on a personal record ladder
          - Choosing the fastest strategy for each fact
          - Building speed on top of real understanding
          - Racing only against yesterday's self, never a classmate
        Practice: Set a friendly one-minute challenge of easy facts and let your child try to
        beat their own score from last time, celebrating any gain.
        Detail: Timed play now that meaning holds: beat-your-own-record ladders, never
        child-versus-child pressure
      Graduation and the Road Ahead
        Topics:
          - Choosing a favourite strategy to teach
          - Running a number talk for the class or mentor
          - Explaining each step clearly to others
          - Reviewing all the strategies learned this year
          - Celebrating durable, understood speed
          - Looking ahead to the next maths adventure
        Practice: Let your child teach the whole family their favourite strategy in a
        five-minute mini-lesson, using a real example.
        Assessment: A gentle final review where the child leads a number talk teaching a chosen
        strategy, revisits the year's key ideas, and celebrates progress, with a friendly
        road-ahead plan instead of a test.
        Detail: Graduation project: each child runs a number talk, teaching their favourite
        strategy, plus final stage mastery check and the road-ahead plan

PROJECTS THE STUDENT BUILDS AND KEEPS

  - The child's own strategy book: every named strategy with their worked example
  - Number-talk leadership: each child regularly explains routes to the class or mentor
  - Beat-your-own-record fluency ladders, tracked across the year
