COMMON QUESTIONS ABOUT THIS COURSE

  For anything about cost, use PART 4 and RULE 1. Do not quote two regions.

  Q: How is this different from abacus or Vedic maths classes?
  A: It rarely transfers to fractions, word problems or algebra, and it fades when practice
  stops. We build number sense instead: strategies the child understands and chooses between.
  The speed arrives a little later and then never leaves, because it is made of understanding.

  Q: What age is right to start?
  A: Ages 5-10, and the mentor meets each child at their actual stage rather than their age.
  Five-year-olds start with quantity games and bonds; nine-year-olds might start at the
  strategy toolkit. The playful diagnostic in the free demo places every child accurately.
  (Agent note: the free demo is a waiting list with no fixed date. The Priority Live Demo is a
  guaranteed class today or tomorrow, booked at https://learn.modernagecoders.com/priority-demo
  . Offer both, as RULE 3 says.)

  Q: Will my child actually enjoy this, or is it drilling in disguise?
  A: Enjoyment is the engine of the whole method: number talks, strategy tournaments,
  beat-your-own-record ladders and games carry every class. Parents consistently tell us their
  children wait for these classes, which sounds impossible for arithmetic until you watch one.
  That is what the free demo is for. (Agent note: the free demo is a waiting list with no fixed
  date. The Priority Live Demo is a guaranteed class today or tomorrow, booked at
  https://learn.modernagecoders.com/priority-demo . Offer both, as RULE 3 says.)

  Q: My child counts on fingers past age 7. Is that a problem this fixes?
  A: Yes, and gently. Finger counting past grade 2 means number bonds never became automatic,
  so every calculation starts from scratch. We rebuild the bonds through games until known
  facts replace counting, without ever shaming the fingers on the way.

  Q: Does this replace school maths or run alongside it?
  A: Alongside, and underneath: number sense is the foundation school maths quietly assumes.
  Children in this course typically find school arithmetic suddenly easy, which buys the
  confidence that changes everything else.

  Q: How much practice is needed between classes?
  A: About ten minutes a day of assigned play, a game, a strategy challenge, a number talk with
  a parent. Small daily doses beat weekend marathons for fluency building, and ten minutes
  keeps it joyful.

  Q: How is my child assessed, and is the certificate just for attending?
  A: No. A problem set follows every class with written feedback, monthly reviews deliberately
  mix new material with earlier topics so nothing is forgotten, and the course ends with a
  final assessment (a friendly speed-and-accuracy check of everything learned). Passing earns
  the certificate; falling short earns focused revision and a free retest. We measure real
  understanding, not attendance.

  Q: Can we try it before paying?
  A: Yes. Every child starts with a free live demo class that doubles as the playful
  diagnostic, no card details, no obligation.

COMMON QUESTIONS ABOUT THIS COURSE

  For anything about cost, use PART 4 and RULE 1. Do not quote two regions.

  Q: What does this MERN stack course cover?
  A: The full JavaScript product craft in order: web and JavaScript foundations, React with
  production patterns, then Node and Express APIs designed professionally, MongoDB modeled with
  judgment, authentication done safely, and full-stack integration where the halves become one
  deployed product. A finale month ships a complete MERN capstone and sits the final exam.

  Q: How long does it take to learn the MERN stack properly?
  A: Ten months of teaching at 2 live classes a week plus 4 to 6 hours of practice, with two
  more months in hand for learners who need them. The three teaching phases build the skill and
  its real-world application; the finale month ships a capstone and sits the final exam.

  Q: How am I assessed? Is the certificate just for attending?
  A: No. Problem sets follow every class with written feedback, monthly reviews deliberately
  mix new material with earlier topics, each phase ends with a cumulative exam, and the course
  ends with a final exam: a practical build plus written questions from the whole syllabus.
  Passing earns the certificate; falling short earns focused revision and a free retest.

  Q: Is MERN still relevant, or should I learn Next.js instead?
  A: Both, in order: MERN teaches the separated architecture that makes you understand what
  frameworks like Next.js later collapse for convenience. Job listings still name MERN
  constantly, and a developer who owns this stack picks up Next.js in a week, the reverse is
  rarely true. Our React and full-stack courses cover the Next.js road explicitly.

ABOUT THE PROGRAMME

  Schools assume children can format a document, build a presentation and manage their files,
  but nobody actually teaches it. This live online course does, properly, for children aged 7
  to 12: Windows fundamentals and tidy file habits, digital art with the built-in creative
  tools, real Microsoft Word skills, PowerPoint presentations with restraint and style, first
  Excel spreadsheets with formulas and charts, and OneNote and Teams, the tools their school
  life increasingly runs on. Everything is project-based: children produce school reports,
  posters, family newsletters, quiz presentations, pocket-money trackers and a final integrated
  project they present at demo day. The pace is honest and kid-sized: five months of teaching
  at two live classes a week, with a sixth month in hand for children who need more practice.
  Classwork in every session, a small homework task after every class, a mixed challenge at
  each month's end, and a final exam, a project demo plus a friendly practical test, that
  decides the certificate. Real skills, really tested, immediately useful at school.

  - Current tools, honestly taught: Windows 11, the free Office web apps, Photos and Clipchamp,

COMMON QUESTIONS ABOUT THIS COURSE

  For anything about cost, use PART 4 and RULE 1. Do not quote two regions.

  Q: What will my child learn in this course?
  A: Real, school-ready digital skills: Windows confidence and tidy file habits, photo editing
  and first videos with the free Photos and Clipchamp apps, professional documents in Word,
  presentations with actual design sense in PowerPoint, first spreadsheets with formulas and
  charts in Excel, and OneNote and Teams for school organization.

  Q: Which age group is this designed for?
  A: Ages 7 to 12, with batches grouped by age so the pace and examples fit the room. No prior
  computer experience is needed; the course starts at the desktop and the mouse and builds up
  patiently.

  Q: How long does it take a child to learn Microsoft Office?
  A: To real, school-ready capability: 5 months at 2 live classes a week plus an hour or two of
  practice. The course keeps a 6th month in hand for children who need more repetition, with no
  rushing and no penalty. Skills show up at school almost immediately, the first properly
  formatted report usually appears within month 2.

  Q: How is my child assessed? Is the certificate just for attending?
  A: No. There is classwork in every session, a small homework task after every class, and a
  mixed challenge at the end of each month that deliberately revisits earlier skills so they
  stop fading. The course ends with a final practical exam plus a project demo. Passing earns
  the certificate; a child who falls short gets focused revision and a free retest. Gentle in
  tone, real in standard.

  Q: Does my child need computer experience before starting?
  A: No. Everything builds step by step from there.

  Q: What software does my child need at home?
  A: A Windows computer with internet is enough. The free Office web versions of Word,
  PowerPoint, Excel and OneNote cover the whole course, and we use them alongside free built-in
  tools like Photos, Clipchamp and the Snipping Tool. If your family already has desktop Office
  or Microsoft 365, your child can use that too; nothing needs to be purchased.

  Q: How does this help with school, and what comes next?
  A: The skills map directly to schoolwork: essays and reports in Word, class presentations in
  PowerPoint, and data projects in Excel. Afterwards, many students move into our Scratch or
  kids coding courses, since comfortable computer use makes learning to code much smoother.

  Q: Can my child attend a trial class first?
  A: Yes, the first step for every family is a free demo class, booked at
  learn.modernagecoders.com/contact. There is no commitment attached, and parents can sit in to
  see exactly how the teacher works with kids. (Agent note: the free demo is a waiting list
  with no fixed date. The Priority Live Demo is a guaranteed class today or tomorrow, booked at
  https://learn.modernagecoders.com/priority-demo . Offer both, as RULE 3 says.)

  Q: What do the classes look like?
  A: Each class is a live 1-hour online session with a real teacher guiding a small group,
  never a pre-recorded video. Children practice hands-on in the actual software during class
  and get help the moment they are stuck.

  Q: Will my child receive a certificate?
  A: Yes, and it is earned: the certificate is awarded on passing the final exam, a practical
  test across Word, PowerPoint and Excel plus the integrated project demo, with a free retest
  after revision if the first attempt falls short. Alongside it stands a portfolio of 20+ real
  documents, presentations and spreadsheets.

COMMON QUESTIONS ABOUT THIS COURSE

  For anything about cost, use PART 4 and RULE 1. Do not quote two regions.

  Q: What does the Middle School Mathematics program cover?
  A: The 12 month program builds in four phases: number systems and operations; fractions,
  decimals, percentages and ratios; pre-algebra with equations, functions and graphing; and
  finally geometry, statistics, probability and multi-step problem solving. The aim is to make
  the middle school years the strongest part of a child's maths story.

  Q: Who is this course right for?
  A: A gentle diagnostic in the first weeks means each child starts where their actual
  understanding is, not where their grade label says.

  Q: What does my child need before joining?
  A: Just completed elementary school mathematics, a computer or tablet with internet, and a
  calculator. No coding background is needed, and grade level reading is enough to follow the
  classes comfortably.

  Q: Will this help with school exams and word problems?
  A: Yes. Word problems and multi-step reasoning are treated as core skills throughout, not an
  afterthought: children learn to translate situations into maths before computing. Because the
  course teaches the concepts under every school syllabus, the work transfers directly to
  classroom tests.

  Q: How is progress measured?
  A: Through weekly practice reviewed for method, phase-end checks before new material begins,
  and a running mastery record shared with parents. The final month includes projects and a
  comprehensive review, so you finish with visible evidence of what your child can now do.

  Q: How is my child assessed, and is the certificate just for attending?
  A: No. A problem set follows every class with written feedback, monthly reviews deliberately
  mix new material with earlier topics so nothing is forgotten, each phase ends with a
  cumulative exam, and the course ends with a final exam covering the whole syllabus. Passing
  earns the certificate; falling short earns focused revision and a free retest. We measure
  understanding, not attendance.

Subject area: Kids Coding

PRICE FOR THIS COURSE (quote only the one that applies to the person asking)
  In India, per month:      group Rs 1,499, mini batch Rs 2,999, one to one Rs 4,999
  Outside India, per month: group $100, one to one $150
  Classes: group and mini batch two live classes a week, eight a month; one to one in India one
  live class a week, four a month; one to one outside India two live classes a week, eight a
  month. Each class is one hour.

WHAT THIS COURSE IS

  Minecraft coding classes for kids ages 7-12: live online lessons using block-based MakeCode,
  from first commands to robot agents, auto-farms, and mini-games.

  In one line: The game your child already loves becomes the place they learn to think in code.

ABOUT THE PROGRAMME

  Minecraft has a superpower most parents never see: a built-in coding environment where
  children snap together blocks of code, press run, and watch the game obey. A castle wall
  appears in two seconds. A robot agent plants a farm. A trap springs when someone steps on the
  wrong block. This 4-month live course uses that loop, code it, run it, see it, to teach real
  programming ideas to children aged 7 to 12. Months 1 and 2 build the core: commands, the
  agent robot, loops that build faster than hands ever could, variables, and decisions. Months
  3 and 4 turn those pieces into games: randomness, scores, timers, a full mini-game classmates
  play, and a finishing capstone the student designs. Along the way, older students get to flip
  the same blocks into JavaScript view and see what their program looks like as typed code.
  Every class is live and hands-on. The instructor sets a build challenge, students code their
  own solution while the instructor watches and helps, and each week ends with something
  running in the world that was not there before.

WHAT MAKES THIS COURSE DIFFERENT

  - Coding happens inside Minecraft itself, so the feedback loop is instant and the motivation is
    already installed
  - The agent robot makes loops and conditions physical: children watch their code walk, turn,
    plant, and build block by block
  - Challenges are sized for live classes: every session ends with a working build, not a
    half-finished follow-along
  - Block code is flipped to JavaScript view for curious older kids, so the bridge to typed
    programming is walked, not just mentioned
  - Screen time turns productive: the same game hours now produce farms, machines, and mini-games
    the child engineered
  - Small live batches mean the instructor sees every child's screen and every child's thinking,
    every class

THE LEARNING PATH, STEP BY STEP

  Phase 1: Code that builds: chat commands, the agent robot, then loops, variables, and
  decisions that construct in seconds what hands build in hours
  Phase 2: Code that plays: randomness, scores, timers, and events combined into real
  mini-games, then a student-designed capstone showcased to families

WHAT A STUDENT NEEDS BEFORE STARTING

  Coding experience: None. The course starts from the very first block of code
  Reading: Basic reading comfort, enough to follow labeled blocks. Seven-year-olds who read
    simple sentences do fine
  Minecraft setup: Minecraft Education, which includes the built-in coding editor. We help
    every family set it up before classes start
  Equipment: A computer or iPad that runs Minecraft Education, plus a stable internet
    connection

WHO THIS COURSE IS FOR

  Minecraft fans: Kids who play Minecraft daily and are ready to command it instead of just
    mining in it
  Complete beginners: Children aged 7 to 12 with zero coding exposure who need a first step
    that feels like play
  Restless learners: Kids who resist worksheets but will happily debug a robot farmer for
    twenty minutes
  Future typers: Older kids in the range who are curious what real typed code looks like, met
    here through the JavaScript view
  Screen time worriers: Parents who want existing Minecraft hours converted into planning,
    logic, and finished projects

FULL CURRICULUM, WEEK BY WEEK

  This is the complete teaching plan. Parents can ask about any week.

  ---------------------------------------------------------------
  PHASE 1: CODE THAT BUILDS (MONTHS 1-2, WEEKS 1-8)
  ---------------------------------------------------------------
  From the first chat command to an automated farm: children learn sequencing, loops,

    Month 1: First Commands and the Agent (Weeks 1-4)
      Hello, Code Builder
        Topics:
          - Opening the coding editor inside Minecraft and a tour of the block palette
          - On chat command: making code run when you type a magic word

          - Saving projects so next class starts where this one ended
        Projects built:
          - Magic words: three chat commands that summon a block tower, a splash of flowers, and a
            chicken
        Practice: Invent two new chat commands of your own and draw what each one should do
        before coding it
      The Agent, Your Robot
        Topics:
          - Meeting the agent: the robot that obeys your program
          - Move forward, turn left, turn right: navigating step by step
          - Agent place and agent destroy: building and clearing
          - Sequencing: why the order of blocks changes everything
          - Walking a maze on paper first, then in code
          - Teleporting the agent back when it wanders off
        Projects built:
          - Maze runner: program the agent to walk a maze you built for it, placing a torch at the exit
        Practice: Build a new maze for a classmate's agent and solve theirs, comparing step
        counts
      Loops: Building at Superspeed
        Topics:
          - The repeat block: doing something ten times without ten copies
          - Building a wall with a loop instead of block-by-block
          - Loops inside loops: from a wall to a whole floor
          - Counting carefully: the off-by-one surprise
          - The forever loop and when it is useful
          - Hand-build vs loop-build: racing the same wall both ways
        Projects built:
          - Wall factory: one program that builds a wall of any length, then a full square fort using
            nested loops
        Practice: Use loops to build a staircase to the clouds, then estimate how long it would
        have taken by hand
      Big Builds with Loops
        Topics:
          - Planning a build as layers: what repeats and what does not
          - Pyramids: each layer smaller than the last
          - Hollow shapes: skipping the middle to save blocks
          - Combining agent moves and loops for long structures
          - Debugging a build gone wrong: reading the code out loud
          - Showing your build: a mini tour for the class
        Projects built:
          - Pyramid of Giza: a layered pyramid built entirely by code, with a hollow secret chamber
            inside
        Practice: Design and code one original loop-built monument for the class world
        Assessment: Month 1 build check: the agent completes a fresh maze and a loop-built
        structure, explained block by block

    Month 2: Variables and Decisions (Weeks 5-8)
      Variables: Code That Remembers
        Topics:
          - What a variable is: a labeled box the program remembers
          - A size variable: one number that controls how big the build is
          - Changing a variable while the program runs
          - Counting things: how many blocks the agent has placed
          - Announcing values in chat: the program reports back
          - Naming variables so they explain themselves
        Projects built:
          - Any-size house: one program that builds a house small, medium, or giant by changing a single
            number
        Practice: Add a height variable to your fort program and test it at three different
        values
      Decisions: Code That Checks
        Topics:
          - If and else: teaching the program to choose
          - Agent detect: is there a block in front of me?
          - Obstacle dodging: walk forward, but go around what blocks you
          - Checking what a block is made of before acting
          - Combining checks: if this and not that
          - Predict-then-run: guessing what a decision program will do
        Projects built:
          - Smart explorer: an agent that crosses rough ground by detecting obstacles and stepping around
            them
        Practice: Program a tunnel-digger that stops when it detects water, so nobody floods
        the base
      Events: Code That Reacts
        Topics:
          - On player walk: code that fires when someone steps somewhere
          - On block placed and on block broken
          - Building a pressure-plate trap the coding way
          - Surprise effects: fireworks, sounds, and chat messages
          - Being a fair trap-maker: warnings and escape routes
          - Multiple events in one world without chaos
        Projects built:
          - Trap gauntlet: a walkway with three coded surprises, from harmless confetti to a drop into a
            pool
        Practice: Add a welcome event to the class world that greets any player who arrives at
        your base
      Project Week: The Auto-Farm
        Topics:
          - Automation: teaching the agent a full job, start to finish
          - Till, plant, wait, harvest: the farming loop
          - Combining loops, variables, and detection in one program
          - Testing a long program one section at a time
          - Making the farm bigger without rewriting it
          - Explaining your automation to someone who does not code
        Projects built:
          - Agent auto-farm: a robot farmer that tills the soil, plants crops in rows, and harvests when
            ready
        Practice: Extend your farm with a fence-building routine, then measure how many crops
        one run produces
        Assessment: Month 2 skills check: a live automation challenge solved with loops, a
        variable, and at least one detect decision

  ---------------------------------------------------------------
  PHASE 2: CODE THAT PLAYS (MONTHS 3-4, WEEKS 9-16)
  ---------------------------------------------------------------
  The building skills become game-making skills: randomness, scores, and timers combine into
  real mini-games, and the course ends with a student-designed capstone and a peek at real
  typed code.

    Month 3: Mini-Games (Weeks 9-12)
      Randomness
        Topics:
          - Random numbers: why games need surprise
          - Spawning animals at random positions
          - Random blocks: a patchwork floor no one can predict
          - Hiding treasure somewhere new every game
          - Fair vs unfair randomness in games
          - Testing random code: run it many times, watch the spread
        Projects built:
          - Treasure hunt: a diamond block hidden at a random spot each round, with hot-and-cold chat
            hints
        Practice: Make a random pet generator that spawns one of five animals, and tally twenty
        runs to see the spread
      Keeping Score
        Topics:
          - A score variable that events update
          - Announcing the score in chat after each point
          - Win conditions: first to ten
          - Resetting the game for a fresh round
          - Counting down instead of up: lives
          - Score displays that players actually notice
        Projects built:
          - Collector clash: gather the glowing blocks scattered by code, one point each, first to ten
            wins
        Practice: Add a lives system to your treasure hunt: three wrong digs and the round ends
      Timers and Pressure
        Topics:
          - Countdown timers built from loops and waits
          - Beat the clock: finishing a task before time runs out
          - Announcing time left at the right moments
          - Combining a timer with a score for real tension
          - Rounds: game start, game play, game over
          - Tuning time limits so the game is hard but winnable
        Projects built:
          - Build rush: players race a two-minute timer to copy a target structure, with a code-checked
            finish
        Practice: Playtest your build rush with family and adjust the time limit after two
        rounds
      Project Week: The Arena Game
        Topics:
          - Combining the month: randomness, score, timer, and events in one game
          - Building the arena with your loop skills
          - Rules players can learn in ten seconds
          - Running a game for classmates: host duties
          - Watching players find the fun and the flaws
          - One improvement pass after the first playtest
        Projects built:
          - Falling-floor arena: a coded mini-game where floor sections vanish on a timer and the last
            player standing wins
        Practice: Host two rounds of your arena for classmates and write down the one rule that
        confused people most
        Assessment: Arena game demo: classmates play a full round, then the builder explains
        the timer and event code behind it

    Month 4: The Capstone and the Code Peek (Weeks 13-16)
      Functions: Naming Your Powers
        Topics:
          - Functions: wrapping a build routine in a name
          - One buildTower function used five times
          - Functions with a size input
          - A personal toolkit: your best routines, reusable forever
          - Cleaner programs: reading code made of named pieces
          - Sharing a function with a classmate and using theirs
        Projects built:
          - Village in a minute: houses, paths, and lamp posts, each a function, assembled into a whole
            village program
        Practice: Turn your favorite build from the course into a function and use it three
        times in one world
      The JavaScript Peek
        Topics:
          - Flipping the editor: the same program as blocks and as JavaScript text
          - Finding your loop and your variable in the typed code
          - What brackets, dots, and semicolons are doing
          - Making one tiny change in text view and running it
          - Block coding vs typed coding: same thinking, different clothes
          - Where typed languages lead: Python, JavaScript, and beyond
        Projects built:
          - Two-view build: a fountain program written in blocks, then modified once in JavaScript view
            to change its size
        Practice: Flip three of your old programs to code view and find the repeat loop in each
        one
      Capstone Build Sprint
        Topics:
          - Choosing a capstone: an original game or a grand automation
          - The one-page plan: what it does, what code it needs, what done means
          - Building must-haves first
          - Reusing your own functions and past code honestly
          - Instructor check-in: unblocking the hard part early
          - Trimming the plan when time runs short, without giving up the core
        Projects built:
          - Capstone, part one: the core of an original mini-game or automation, planned and working end
            to end
        Practice: Two 30-minute build sessions at home, each ending with a one-sentence
        progress note
      Finish and Showcase
        Topics:
          - The final bug hunt: testing every part on purpose
          - Polish: sounds, messages, and a proper welcome
          - Writing simple instructions for players
          - Presenting: show the game first, then the code behind the best part
          - Answering questions about your own program
          - What comes next: Python for kids, or Roblox game coding
        Projects built:
          - Finished capstone: an original, tested Minecraft game or automation presented live to
            classmates and families
        Practice: Run your capstone for two family members and collect one compliment and one
        improvement idea from each
        Assessment: Capstone showcase and code Q&A, plus course-completion certificate review

COMMON QUESTIONS ABOUT THIS COURSE

  For anything about cost, use PART 4 and RULE 1. Do not quote two regions.

  Q: Is this course run by Mojang or Microsoft?
  A: No. Modern Age Coders is an independent coding school, and this course is not affiliated
  with, sponsored by, or endorsed by Mojang or Microsoft. We teach coding using Minecraft
  Education and its built-in MakeCode editor, tools Microsoft makes available for exactly this
  kind of learning, but the curriculum and classes are entirely ours.

  Q: Which version of Minecraft do we need? Will our normal Minecraft work?
  A: The course uses Minecraft Education, the school-focused version with the coding editor
  (Code Builder) built in. The regular Bedrock or Java editions your child may already own do
  not include this editor, so Education is required; it runs on Windows, Mac, iPad, and most
  Chromebooks, and needs its own low-cost licence or a school Microsoft 365 Education account.
  Before the batch starts we walk every family through the setup, and we confirm your device
  runs it during the free demo. (Agent note: the free demo is a waiting list with no fixed
  date. The Priority Live Demo is a guaranteed class today or tomorrow, booked at
  https://learn.modernagecoders.com/priority-demo . Offer both, as RULE 3 says.)

  Q: Will my child actually learn coding, or just play Minecraft in class?
  A: Every class is a coding class; Minecraft is the place the code runs, not the activity.
  Students spend sessions writing programs: loops that raise walls, decisions that steer a
  robot, events that trigger traps, timers that run games. The game world is what makes a
  seven-year-old care whether their loop is correct, because a wrong loop builds a crooked
  castle in front of everyone.

  Q: My child already gets too much screen time. Does this add more?
  A: For most families it converts time rather than adds it. The hours a child was already
  spending in Minecraft start producing farms they automated, games they invented, and bugs
  they fixed, which exercises planning and logic in a way passive play does not. Classes are
  one focused hour, and home practice is deliberately kept to one or two hours a week, sized
  for this age group.

  Q: Is 7 too young? My older child is 12, is it too basic?
  A: Both ends of the range are served, differently. Sevens thrive because block coding removes
  typing and spelling from the equation; they drag, snap, and run. Twelves stay stretched
  through harder challenges, functions, and the JavaScript view, where they read and edit their
  own programs as typed code. Batches are grouped by age so the pace fits the room.

  Q: What does my child move on to after this course?
  A: The two most common paths are our Python for kids course, which takes the same ideas into
  the world's most-used typed language, and Roblox game coding, where students script 3D games
  in Luau. The instructor recommends a path for each child at the end of the course based on
  what they gravitated toward.

  Q: How is my child assessed, and is the certificate just for attending?
  A: No. A task follows every class with feedback, monthly reviews deliberately mix new
  material with earlier topics so nothing is forgotten, and the course ends with a friendly
  final assessment of everything learned. Passing earns the certificate; falling short earns
  focused revision and a free retest. We measure real learning, not attendance.

  Q: Can we try a class before enrolling?
  A: Yes, the first demo class is free and carries no obligation. Book it at
  learn.modernagecoders.com/contact or message us on WhatsApp at +91 91233 66161. The demo
  doubles as a tech check: we make sure Minecraft Education runs on your device and answer
  setup questions with a parent present.

  Q: Do parents need to know anything about coding or Minecraft?
  A: No. Many parents tell us that presentation is the first time they understood what the
  course was building all along.

  To enrol, message Shivam Sir on +91 9123366161 or send the parent this link: https://learn.modernagecoders.com/courses/minecraft-coding-for-kids-course
  For a demo: the Priority Live Demo (guaranteed, today or tomorrow) is booked at
  https://learn.modernagecoders.com/priority-demo . The free demo is a waiting list with no fixed date.

WHAT THIS COURSE IS

  MySQL course for college students and professionals: SQL mastery, database design, stored
  procedures, transactions, Python integration and honest admin in 7-8 months.

  In one line: The data layer, owned end to end: SQL fluency, real schema design, the programmable database, and the production habits developers are actually judged on.

ABOUT THE PROGRAMME

  Every application stands on a database, and every serious interview eventually reaches SQL.
  This live online masterclass takes college students and professionals from zero to genuine
  capability in seven months: SQL written fluently, schemas designed rather than accumulated,
  the programmable side of MySQL (views, stored procedures, triggers, transactions), Python
  integration where data becomes application, and the production basics, security, backups and
  performance tuning, that separate developers who use databases from developers databases can
  trust. The scope is deliberately honest. Full database administration, replication clusters,
  multi-cloud failover, is its own profession, and courses that staple it onto a beginner
  syllabus produce neither developers nor DBAs. This course builds the 95% that developers,
  analysts and interviews actually demand, names the DBA path clearly for those who want it
  next, and spends the reclaimed months making the fundamentals genuinely deep: joins that
  never confuse, EXPLAIN read like a native, transactions understood well enough to argue
  about. The pace is honest: seven months at two live classes a week plus three to four hours
  of practice, with an eighth month in hand. Problem sets after every class, monthly mixed
  reviews, and a final exam, practical plus written, that decides the certificate with a free
  retest after revision. Real queries, real design, depth over dopamine.

WHAT MAKES THIS COURSE DIFFERENT

  - Honest scope: the developer 95%, not a stapled-on DBA career track
  - Design is taught as a craft: ER modeling, normalization and constraints, practiced on real
    domains
  - The programmable database gets real weeks: views, procedures, triggers and transactions, not
    a demo each
  - EXPLAIN fluency: performance tuning taught as reading, reasoning and measuring
  - Ends integrated: MySQL driven from Python, with security, backups and tuning as habits
  - Real assessment: weekly problem sets, monthly mixed reviews, and a final exam that decides
    the certificate, with focused revision and a free retest

THE LEARNING PATH, STEP BY STEP

  Phase 1: SQL foundations (Months 1-2): setup, DDL, DML and SELECT mastery on real datasets
  Phase 2: Design and joins (Months 3-4): relationships, joins without fear, subqueries and set
  operations, and schema design done properly
  Phase 3: The programmable database (Months 5-6): views, indexes, stored procedures, triggers,
  transactions and Python integration
  Phase 4: Production month (Month 7): security and backups, performance tuning with EXPLAIN,
  and the capstone exam

WHAT A STUDENT NEEDS BEFORE STARTING

  Coding experience: None for the SQL core; the Python integration weeks are guided and
    beginner-safe
  Equipment: A computer with a stable internet connection; MySQL Community Server and every

  Age: 18+; college students, graduates and working professionals
  Time commitment: 2 live classes plus 3-4 hours of practice a week

COMMON QUESTIONS ABOUT THIS COURSE

  For anything about cost, use PART 4 and RULE 1. Do not quote two regions.

  Q: Is this course only about writing SQL queries?
  A: No, and that is the point. Queries are phase 1; the course continues into schema design as
  a craft, the programmable database, views, stored procedures, triggers and transactions,
  Python integration, and the production habits of security, backups and EXPLAIN-driven
  performance tuning. What it deliberately does not staple on is the full DBA career track,
  replication clusters and multi-cloud failover, which is its own profession and is named
  honestly as a next path.

  Q: How long does it take to learn MySQL properly?
  A: Seven months at 2 live classes a week plus 3 to 4 hours of practice covers the developer
  95%: SQL fluency, design, the programmable database and production basics. The course keeps
  an eighth month in hand for learners who need more repetition, no rushing and no penalty.
  Twelve-month database courses are stretched; two-week ones are demos.

  Q: How am I assessed? Is the certificate just for attending?
  A: No. Problem sets follow every class with written feedback, monthly reviews deliberately
  mix new topics with earlier ones, each phase ends with an exam, and the course ends with a
  final exam, a practical build plus written questions from the whole syllabus. Passing earns
  the certificate; falling short earns focused revision and a free retest.

  Q: Do I need programming experience to start?
  A: No. SQL is taught from the first statement and is one of the friendliest languages to
  begin with. The Python integration weeks in phase 3 are guided and assume nothing; students
  who already code simply move faster there.

  Q: Which MySQL version and tools do you teach?
  A: Current MySQL 8 with MySQL Workbench, all free Community editions, plus the command line
  where professionals actually live. Everything taught transfers to MariaDB and, concepts-wise,
  to PostgreSQL; SQL fluency is portable by design.

  Q: How does this help with placements and interviews?
  A: SQL rounds are near-universal in data and software hiring, and they test exactly what this
  course drills: joins under pressure, subqueries, aggregation edge cases, schema design
  judgment and transaction reasoning. The monthly mixed reviews keep older material
  interview-fresh, and the capstone gives you a designed, tuned, documented database to talk
  through.

  the demo is best on your real problem. (Agent note: the free demo is a waiting list with no
  fixed date. The Priority Live Demo is a guaranteed class today or tomorrow, booked at
  https://learn.modernagecoders.com/priority-demo . Offer both, as RULE 3 says.)

  Q: Are classes live or recorded?
  A: Live, always: small groups where your actual SQL gets read and corrected in real time,
  never pre-recorded videos. Database judgment is built under feedback; a video cannot see your
  execution plan.

ABOUT THE PROGRAMME

  Behind Instagram, Spotify and every game leaderboard sits the same quiet skill: SQL, the
  language of data. This live online course teaches it properly to students aged 13 to 18, from
  the first SELECT to real database design, in five honest months. SQL is one of the
  highest-value skills per hour of learning in all of computing: the language is compact, the
  concepts are learnable at 13, and the skill stays current for decades. The arc is practical
  from the first week: students query and build real databases about things they care about,
  music libraries, game inventories, school clubs, then learn the query toolkit (functions,
  aggregation, subqueries), real design (relationships, joins, ER diagrams, constraints), the
  power features professionals lean on (views, stored procedures, transactions, indexes), and
  finish by securing a database and connecting it to Python, where data becomes an actual
  application. The capstone is a complete, well-designed, connected database project defended
  at demo day. The pace is honest: five months at two live classes a week plus two to three
  hours of practice, with a sixth month in hand for students who need more time. Homework after
  every class, monthly mixed reviews that reach back deliberately, and a final exam that
  decides the certificate, with a free retest after revision. Real queries, real design, depth
  over dopamine.

WHAT MAKES THIS COURSE DIFFERENT

  - Honest length: SQL fundamentals to real design in 5 months, not a stretched year

  - The professional features that matter: views, procedures, transactions and indexes, each

  - Ends connected: MySQL driven from Python, so the database becomes an application

COURSE 94 OF 122: OLYMPIAD MATHEMATICS: IOQM, INMO AND AMC PREPARATION

Subject area: Olympiad Mathematics
Designed for: Teens

Course length: 12 months (48 weeks), joinable any month
Time needed: 2 live classes/week + weekly problem sets and timed mocks

PRICE FOR THIS COURSE (quote only the one that applies to the person asking)

  Outside India, per month: group $100, one to one $150

WHAT THIS COURSE IS

  Live online olympiad mathematics for serious students: number theory, algebra, combinatorics
  and geometry taught as proof-based problem solving, aimed at IOQM and INMO in India and the
  AMC and AIME internationally.

  In one line: The four olympiad pillars taught as real proof-based problem solving, for students who have outgrown school maths.

ABOUT THE PROGRAMME

  Olympiad mathematics is a different subject from school mathematics wearing the same name.
  School maths asks you to apply a method you were just shown. Olympiad maths hands you a
  problem you have never seen, gives you no method, and asks you to construct an argument that
  is airtight. Students who top their class routinely struggle at first, and that is normal,
  because nothing in the school syllabus trains this. This course teaches the four pillars that
  every olympiad is built on: number theory, algebra, combinatorics and geometry. Each is
  taught for genuine understanding and then drilled on real past problems, because olympiad
  ability is built by attempting hard problems and failing productively, not by watching
  solutions. It is aimed at both the Indian and international ladders. In India the path runs
  through IOQM, the Indian Olympiad Qualifier in Mathematics, on to INMO and the training camp
  beyond it. Internationally students target the AMC 10 and AMC 12, then AIME. The formats
  differ, and we prepare for each specifically, but the underlying skill is the same: reading a
  problem properly, finding the idea, and writing an argument that survives scrutiny. Proof is
  taught explicitly from the start. Most students arrive able to find an answer but unable to
  justify it, and at INMO level the justification is the entire mark. We fix that early,
  because a correct answer with a hand-waving argument scores close to nothing.

WHAT MAKES THIS COURSE DIFFERENT

  - All four pillars taught properly: number theory, algebra, combinatorics and geometry, not
    just contest tricks
  - Proof writing taught explicitly from the start, because at INMO level the argument is the
    mark, not the answer
  - Prepared for both ladders: IOQM and INMO in India, AMC 10, AMC 12 and AIME internationally
  - Built on real past problems, since olympiad ability comes from productive failure on hard
    problems
  - Students are taught to sit with a problem instead of giving up after two minutes, which is
    the actual skill
  - Live, small batches where solutions are critiqued line by line for rigour, not just marked
    right or wrong

THE LEARNING PATH, STEP BY STEP

  Phase 1: Proof technique and number theory, the natural entry point into olympiad thinking
  Phase 2: Algebra and combinatorics, including inequalities and counting arguments
  Phase 3: Geometry, then full contest simulation for IOQM, INMO and the AMC or AIME

WHAT A STUDENT NEEDS BEFORE STARTING

  Title: What Your Child Needs to Start

WHO THIS COURSE IS FOR

  Title: Who This Course Is For

FULL CURRICULUM, WEEK BY WEEK

  This is the complete teaching plan. Parents can ask about any week.

  ---------------------------------------------------------------
  PHASE 1: PROOF TECHNIQUE AND NUMBER THEORY
  ---------------------------------------------------------------
  How to argue rigorously, then the pillar that best rewards it.

    Months 1 to 2: Proof and Foundations (Weeks 1-8)
      What Counts as a Proof
        Topics:
          - The difference between checking cases and proving a statement
          - Direct proof, and writing it so every step is justified
          - Proof by contradiction
          - Proof by contrapositive, and when it is easier
          - Reading a written solution critically and finding the gap
        Projects built:
          - Write five full proofs and have every line challenged in class
        Practice: Prove supplied statements and rewrite them after critique
      Induction and Invariants
        Topics:
          - Mathematical induction, including strong induction
          - Common induction errors that void the proof
          - Invariants and monovariants, and the problems that hide them
          - Extremal arguments: taking the largest or smallest case
          - Recognising which technique a problem is inviting
        Projects built:
          - Solve a set of invariant problems and articulate the invariant explicitly in each
        Practice: 20 induction and invariant problems
        Assessment: A proof-writing assessment marked on rigour, not just the final answer
      Number Theory
        Topics:
          - Divisibility, GCD and the Euclidean algorithm
          - Primes, factorisation and the fundamental theorem of arithmetic
          - Modular arithmetic and congruences
          - Fermat's little theorem and Euler's theorem
          - Diophantine equations at olympiad level
        Projects built:
          - Solve a graded ladder of number theory problems from IOQM level upward
        Practice: 40 number theory problems across the difficulty range
        Assessment: Timed number theory paper under contest conditions

  ---------------------------------------------------------------
  PHASE 2: ALGEBRA AND COMBINATORICS
  ---------------------------------------------------------------
  The two pillars that most often decide an IOQM or AMC score.

    Months 3 to 5: Algebra (Weeks 9-20)
      Polynomials and Functional Equations
        Topics:
          - Polynomial roots, factorisation and Vieta's formulas
          - Symmetric functions and their uses
          - Functional equations and the standard substitution strategies
          - Recognising the structure hidden in an ugly expression
          - Writing algebraic arguments cleanly
        Projects built:
          - Work a set of Vieta and functional equation problems from past papers
        Practice: 30 algebra problems building in difficulty
      Inequalities
        Topics:
          - AM-GM and its many disguises
          - Cauchy-Schwarz
          - Rearrangement and Chebyshev
          - Normalisation and substitution tactics
          - Knowing when to stop searching for a slicker method
        Projects built:
          - Prove a graded set of inequalities, each with a fully justified argument
        Practice: 30 inequality problems
        Assessment: Timed algebra paper under contest conditions
      Combinatorics
        Topics:
          - Counting properly: permutations, combinations and overcounting
          - The pigeonhole principle and its surprisingly deep uses
          - Inclusion and exclusion
          - Bijections and counting the same set two ways
          - Introductory graph theory and games
        Projects built:
          - Solve a counting problem two different ways and reconcile the results
        Practice: 35 combinatorics problems
        Assessment: Timed combinatorics paper

  ---------------------------------------------------------------
  PHASE 3: GEOMETRY AND FULL CONTEST SIMULATION
  ---------------------------------------------------------------
  The pillar students most often avoid, then the contests themselves rehearsed properly.

    Months 6 to 9: Geometry (Weeks 21-36)
      Synthetic Geometry
        Topics:
          - Angle chasing done systematically rather than hopefully
          - Cyclic quadrilaterals and the power of a point
          - Similar triangles and ratio arguments
          - The classical centres and their properties
          - Drawing an accurate diagram, which solves more problems than any theorem
        Projects built:
          - Solve a ladder of synthetic geometry problems with full written proofs
        Practice: 35 geometry problems from contest papers
      Advanced Geometry Techniques
        Topics:
          - Coordinate geometry as a fallback when synthetic stalls
          - Trigonometric methods in geometry
          - Homothety and transformations
          - Choosing between synthetic, coordinate and trigonometric attacks
          - Recognising when a problem is resisting the method rather than you
        Projects built:
          - Attack the same hard problem three ways and compare which was cleanest
        Practice: 25 problems requiring a deliberate choice of method
        Assessment: Timed geometry paper
      Mixed Problem Solving
        Topics:
          - Problems that do not announce their topic
          - Deciding quickly which pillar a problem belongs to
          - Working when the first idea fails, and the second
          - Managing frustration, which is a genuine competition skill
          - Building a personal record of techniques that worked
        Projects built:
          - Weekly mixed problem sets with no topic labels
        Practice: Mixed sets under time

    Months 10 to 12: Contest Simulation (Weeks 37-48)
      IOQM and AMC Format Training
        Topics:
          - The IOQM format and how to pace it
          - AMC 10 and AMC 12 pacing, and the scoring implications of guessing
          - Answer-extraction techniques for short-answer formats
          - Knowing when to abandon a question and return
          - Accuracy under time, where most marks are actually lost
        Projects built:
          - Full timed IOQM and AMC papers every week
        Practice: Weekly full papers with question-by-question review
      INMO and AIME Level, and Peak Form
        Topics:
          - The step up to full written proofs at INMO level
          - AIME format and its particular demands
          - Writing a complete solution under time pressure
          - Partial credit: how to secure marks on a problem you cannot finish
          - Contest-day routine, sleep and nerves
        Projects built:
          - Full INMO-style and AIME-style papers, marked on rigour
        Practice: Continuous full-paper cycle with detailed feedback
        Assessment: Final full mock contest, marked as an examiner would, with an honest
        readiness assessment

  Homework: A task or problem set after every class, and a monthly mixed-review assignment that

  In India, per month:      group Rs 1,499, mini batch Rs 2,999, one to one Rs 4,999
  Outside India, per month: group $100, one to one $150

WHAT THIS COURSE IS

  Master Orange Data Mining in 24 live classes for college students: reproducible workflows,
  feature engineering, model selection with nested validation, explainability, clustering, text
  mining, time series and a defended analytics capstone, plus the Python bridge to pandas and
  scikit-learn.

  In one line: Cover a full data mining syllabus on a visual canvas, then defend it: rigorous validation, feature engineering, explainability, clustering, text and time series, and a capstone that reproduces from raw data on someone else's machine.

ABOUT THE PROGRAMME

  Data mining appears in almost every computer science, IT, statistics, business analytics and
  bioinformatics programme, and it is routinely taught as a list of algorithm names to memorise
  before an exam. This course teaches it as a practice. Orange is free, open source machine
  learning and data visualisation software developed at the Bioinformatics Laboratory, Faculty
  of Computer and Information Science, University of Ljubljana, released under the GNU GPL
  version 3 or later. It was built for teaching machine learning and data mining to university
  students, and it is used in real research work. You assemble analysis by connecting widgets
  on a canvas, which removes the syntax overhead and puts the entire course budget into method:
  how to prepare data defensibly, how to select a model without fooling yourself, and how to
  explain what the model did. Across 24 live classes you work through the six default widget
  sets, Data, Transform, Visualize, Model, Evaluate and Unsupervised, and then into the add-on
  ecosystem that makes Orange genuinely useful for project work: Text for corpus analysis, Time
  Series for temporal data, Explain for model interpretation, Associate for rule mining, Geo
  for spatial data, and Fairness for auditing. You will build classification and regression
  pipelines, use Preprocess inside the modelling loop so that scaling and imputation are fitted
  on training folds rather than leaked across them, compare learners under identical cross
  validation in Test and Score, tune with Parameter Fitter, read ROC, precision-recall and
  calibration properly, and use Explain Model and Permutation Importance to answer the question
  a viva always asks: why did it predict that? The course is deliberately not a dead end at the
  canvas. Orange is written in Python and installable from PyPI as Orange3, and the Python
  Script widget exposes real Python inside a workflow with the incoming data available in your
  namespace. Two classes are spent on that bridge, so students moving on to pandas and
  scikit-learn carry the concepts across rather than starting again. Every class is taught live
  in a small batch by a working practitioner, the same mentorship-first method Modern Age
  Coders has used since 2020 to teach 10,000+ students across 25+ countries. You finish with 24
  reproducible workflows, a capstone that runs end to end from a raw file, and an exported
  report you can put in front of an examiner, a recruiter or a project guide.

WHAT MAKES THIS COURSE DIFFERENT

  - Built for defensible work, not demos: reproducibility, leakage control and honest validation
    are graded requirements from Phase 1, not closing remarks.
  - Covers a full university data mining syllabus, preprocessing, classification, regression,
    evaluation, clustering, dimensionality reduction, association rules, text and time series,
    with a running artefact for each.
  - Explainability is a full class, not a mention: Explain Model, Explain Prediction, Permutation
    Importance and ICE, so you can answer why a prediction happened.
  - The Python bridge is taught explicitly: Orange is a Python library, the Python Script widget
    runs real Python inside the canvas, and the same models exist in scikit-learn.
  - Free and open source under the GNU GPL v3 or later, so nothing in your final year project
    depends on a licence you lose after graduation.
  - Capstone standard is reproduction: your workflow must rerun from the raw file in a clean
    session, on a machine that is not yours.

WHAT A STUDENT NEEDS BEFORE STARTING

  Device: A laptop or desktop running Windows, macOS or Linux capable of installing Orange,

  Coding experience: None required. The entire course can be completed without writing code.

  Maths background: Comfort with school-level statistics, averages, percentages, basic
